From the Observer, December 11, 1853. T11E STATUS QUO ON THE DANUBE.

The position of both armies on the Danube remains unchanged. They may also remain in that condition through the winter þÿ if the " collective note" of England, France, Prussia and Austria, should succeed in its object, the obtainmerit of an armistice. The Russians possess the whole of the left hank of that river, with the exception þÿ and it is a most important one þÿ of Kalafat. This strategic post is held firmly by the Turks ; and up to the present time, no accounts have been received of any attempts on the part of their adversary to dislodge them. Meanwhile the winter has set in with great severity ; and though military operations are riot necessarily thereby suspended, they ate necessarily not a little impeded. It is now perceived, however, that the occupation of 01tenitza by the Turkish forces was a mere feint to draw off the observation of the Russians from Kalafat; and that the three successive repulses sustained by the latter, enabled Omar Pasha to establish his left wing in a formidable position, flanked by deep entrenchments in the vicinity of the latter tow n, which, it should he added, commands the high roads from Austria to YVallnehia. and so checks any probable irruption of the Austrians in aid of the Russians, should the latter sustain a still more disastrous defeat than those they sustained before Oltenitza. This fact explains the cause why the Tuiks crossed the Danube in the first instance ; why, in the second, they held such an apparently unim-

portant position as Oltenitza for so long a period, and against such great odds ; and. in the third, why they retreated across the river after having repelled so bravely the foe, when, as it would appear, the high-road to Bucharest was almost wholly open to them, and their march thither seemed likely to he little more than a military promenade. The next move in the great game now plavirig is not to be easily predicted ; because of the introduction of what astronomers term " a disturbing force." in the calculation of the chances. Under ordinary circumstances, it is demonstrable that the power which was in the fittest þÿcondition thai is to say, in the most forward state of preparation þÿ would cross the Danube first at two or nioie points; that it would then converge towards a common centre; and finally that it would endeavour to decide the campaign in a pitched battle or in a series of divisional encounters, in which all the strength ol each would he brought into full play. On the pat t of the Turks it is not difficult to foresee that this " common centre" would be Bucharest; and that their combined action would lie directed to drive the Russians into the valley of the Carpathian mountains. In such case the latter would only escape from Wallachia to enter Hungary þÿ an alternative similar to that of Scvlla and Chnrvbdis; inasmuch as the presence of a demoralised fugitive Russian army in Hungary would he followed inevitably by an insurrection of the Magyars, in which the Russians already destroyed as

as nn offensive force, would infallibly be cut to pieces by the infuriate peasantry, in revenge for their frightful excesses during the late Hungarian revolutionary war. On the part of the Russians, it is more than probable that the " centre" in question would be Varna, as suggested in The Observer of last Sunday ; in consequence of that important post being the key of all maiitime communication with Constantinople, as well as of its being the best adapted of all the ports on the Black Sea. in respect to safety and in respect to defensibilitv, to form what the French term a succursale, or supplementary harbour to Sebastopol and Odessa. The possession of Varna, besides giving Russia a direct searoad to the Crimea, whence she draws her chief supplies, and where she has her most important dockyards, would also t'ive het in a sense the command of the Balkan passes, bv enabling Iter to turn the flanks of the Turkish forces, now encamped at Shumla, when her strength or her strategy admitted of the movement. Now, however, it would seem as if the hostile action of both powers was paralysed þÿ at least in so far as outward appearances are concerned, by the last diplomatic noveltv þÿ namely, the new "collective note." It is true that this note has not suspended the armaments of Russia þÿ still hss has it moderated the conscription of the unhappy serfs of that country, of the unfortunate people of Roland, or even of the luckless Jews who dwell in tins hyperbotean region; neither

has it affected the enrolment of recruits, pro oris etfocis, in Turkey proper, whither the Asiatic hordes ate pouring in a full tide, to fight as thev did of yore for Islam. But Omai Pasha, it is distinctly stated, has had orders to remain quiet on the right bank of the Danube as well as on the left ; whilst it is certain that Gortscliakoff and the Russians are doing, or þÿ to speak bv the card þÿ have been recently doing nothing. Nevertheless there can be little doubt that the "note" in question will meet the same fate as its predecessors, namely, rejection. Indeed it is generally believed already that it has 110 serious object ; and that its aim is to obtain time þÿ in other words, to place the future in the "chapter nf accidents." and trust to Pimprevu In the meantime, while the world waits, it would he as well for those wealihv Jews in Western Europe who furnish money to Russia to carry out this atrocious war, to cast their eyes upon the persecutions to which that power subjects tier co-religionists. Once in a way the Hebrew race was bellicose in the extreme; since the "curse," however, their courage has become emasculated ; and though they will cheat to any extent, they will fight not at all Under these circumstances it is a cruelty unspeakable on the part of Russia to compel these poor cowards into her armies: while it is a disgrace to the Jewish capitalists of Europe, who are " hand in glove' wnh European despotism in all its lorms, to stand by and see this persecution
without moving a muscle to save them. It is, in fact, Hamnn in the Court of Ahasuerus in this the nineteenth ccnturv.

AUSTRIA. VIENNA. Dec. 2. Letters from the frontier stale that the levy now going on in Russia is not the ordinary recruiting, as has been asserted. So many men were never before seized, so much severity was never before resorted to. and so many children (boys of twelve years of age) were never before taken from their parents to be sent to the regiments. The Austrian Government having learned that it had been publicly announced in London, with a semblance of authority, that the Four Powers had made a kind of alliance favourable to Turkey, has lost not a moment in setting itself risght with Russia It lias caused to be published at Vienna that only a collective note had been drawn up, and that no mutual pledge had been given to enforce its acceptance. It is sad indeed to see how things are managed at Vienna I While matters of such vast European importance are pending, t he Reichsrath is employed in pre paring plans for a more complete return to the ancient system. The avowed object of Government is to eradicate the new fangled ideas from the brains of the lieges, hut it might just as well imitate Canute and bid the tide not to rise. Heads innumerable may be laid low by the hands of the executioner, but the current of popular opinion has set in so strongly that it cannot be stayed for any length of time. The Ultramontane party seems intent on increasing the general eon fusion, and even here Government begins to see and feel that the emancipation of I tic Roman Catholic Church was a political blun-
der.

PRUSSIA. BERLIN, Dec 2 The panic which was produced some four or five months hack by a statement of the Aftenblatt that Russia intended to station 30 000 men in Finland, although written down at the time as a chimera, turns out to be true, on the authority of the seme-official So. Tiilning. It appears that not only Revel and Riga have received 12.000 men of the picked grenadiers, hut also that 16,0h0 men have been added to the usual garrison of Finland, 12,000 strong. Of this last addition 8 900 are stationed in Bomarsund, on the island of Aland, over against Stockholm. 10,000 sailors are concentrated at Helsingfors, and nine ships of the line are appointed to that station, so that they may be ready to put out to sea earlier than they would be able to do from Cronstadt. Not long ago a Russian vessel of war appeared off the southern coast of Gothland (where the Swedes are fortifying their harbour), and making signals of distress, put into the port and sent on shore for provisions, to be supplied with which the crew was in urgent want. The rest of the day was occupied in carefully noting the bearings, soundings, &c., as well as the apparent strength of the fortifications; and when next morning the provisions were 1 brought down to the harbour, " ship in distress" had put out to sea þÿ Ibid.

A NEW COMPOUND FOR ARTIFICIAL GUMS. It has long been a desideratum amongst scientific dental practitioners to discover a substance that would not undergo any decomposition in the mouth, when employed to represent the human gum, in mounting artificial teeth upon gold or platina plates. . In many of these cases the dentist was called upon to restore the contour of the mouth and face, which had been impaired, either by absorption after extraction, by accident, or disease. The tusk of the hippopotamus, dyed to represent the gum in colour, was formerly used for this purpose, which in most consti tutions. particularly where there were acid secretions of the mouth, underwent rapid de composition. This defect was, in a measure, obviated bv the introduction of porcelain teeth with the gum attached ; but the great difficulty, the length of time, and the nicety required in accurately fitting these teeth to the plate and at their lateral edges, so as to prevent the secretions from the saliva and small particles of food lodging in the interstices, was, in some cases, insurmountable. This also was, to some extent, obviated by having the teeth manufactured ir.to blocks, the gums and teeth being thus carved together, and they were then riveted to metalic plates in separate pieces. Although this much improved their appearance, similar objections existed as to the lodgment of foreign matter in the interstices ; and, up to a recent period, the ingenuity and skill of surgeon dentists was vainly taxed to supply a remedy.

This, however, has now been permanently obviated by the invention of Dr. Allen, of America, who has secured a patent for his j discovery in this country, and has selected Mr. Robinson to introduce the discovery in England. This new and valuable process of continuous gums consists in fusing the teeth ; to the plate by means of a metallic and mineral compound, whereby a metallic union is formed between the teeth and plate, there being no seam or crevice for the lodgment of foreign substances The loss of substance, either from absorption, disease or otherwise, ean be readily replaced, and the contour of the face and mouth preserved or perfectly restored to its original condition ; the imitation of nature is admirable, and the new invention combines durability, strength, and þÿcleanliness some of the most important considerations in artificial teeth. Mr. Robinson, in the presence nf a number of medical and scientific gentlemen, explained the whole of the details of this new invention a few nights since at his residence in Gower-street, and fused the new metallic compound in the laborntory furnace, producing a perfect and permanent resemblance to the human teeth and gums. þÿ Ibid

Eroin the number of deaths occurring daily, it is to be seen that the same forms no scale whereby any judgment can he formed as to augmentation or diminution of the fell disease, as on one day the table of mortality indicates a number which would lead us to hope that the malady was disappearing, while on the next day the increase sets a blight to that hope, and leaves us despairing þÿ to place our trust in Him, who alone has the power to define the limit of chastisement of which tins scourge is the lash, and by which we are to atone for our deeds and iniquities. From information we have been able to gather, it would seem that this affliction is not confined to 8t. Thomas ; for the Quays and small Islands in our immediate neighbourhood appear lo be stricken in like manner, only that their case is more to be deplored, as the few inhabitants who live upon them are void of those means to allay their suffering and distress, which a populace town like ours naturally possesses. It is, therefore, painful to learn of the circumstances atten dant with mortality at such places as Jos-van-Dykcs, Loango, and Thatch Island, þÿ the excess of which has, it is said with a few rare þÿ exceptions þÿ depopulated those places ; leaving, in many instances, the dead unburied. Jos-van-Dykes is an Island belonging to the Virgin Islands group,
and a dependency of Great Britain. How comes it. then, that dependencies

claiming allegiance to so great and powerful a nation become so thoroughly uncared for, that during a catastrophe of this nature, the inhabitants are so totally destitute of every succour, and so backward in the scale of civilization, that we are credibly informed that of the few who received a christian burial there, the partitions of some of the cottages standing had to be torn down to make Coffins of. This is a subject warranting reflection, and ought to the Duke of Newcastle be another bit of Choral on which to bite. The season is unfortunately unpropitious for this epidemic, as stormy Northerly winds and chilling rains will bring with them swampy gutters, wet streets, and cold piercing þÿnights premiums to diseases of which cramps, spasms, and weakened bowels are the fore warning symptoms. Warmth of body may with propriety he considered at such a period a rule, which should not only be observed by those whose better knowledge naturally prompts them to adopt, hut one, which those who have undertaken to become the temporary guardians of the poor, should seek to impress upon their wards, as far as it is sometimes possible, to bestow good counsel on those who are often indifferent to their own benefits. Warm feet, avoiding being caught in the rain, and paramount lo all, early hours at night, so as to evade the night air and heavy dews, may he the saving at this calamitous tune of many a life, which regardless of these precautions, may easily He found 'still in death' in the morning. An unusual activity continues with the Board of Health, as well with other individuals, whose humane feelings prompt them to lend their aid and means to render comfort to the poor and needy. In evidence of this, many gentlemen in this city we believe have undertaken at their own cost to make hurriedly, and sup-

ply, grass beds to the Hospitals, and to the houses of the indigent. Soup shops have within a few days been started, where the needy can he provided with nourishment, 'revisions in considerable quantities have also been sent to the Tents for those who have taken refuge there. The Treatment of the Cholera. Mr. E. W. Lane, the well-known Eastern traveller and Orientalist, has communicated the following method of treat- Cairo in 1848, when the ing Asiatic cholera: " While cholera residing in was raging there, 1 was informed that an Englishman in a small neighbouring village had effected a speedy and perfect cure in every case of that disease which he had an opportunity of treating. The number of the cases was G2, and many ot them were very malignant ; and 1 subsequently Learnt that his mode of treatment had been practised with equal success in Spain, Constantinople, and India, and was never followed bv typhus or typhoid fever, which proved fatal in many cases when the cholera itself had been subdued by other means. 1'pon applying to him 1 received the following directions, which I practised in a few cases which afterwards occurred in my house and elsewhere, and with invariable success. It the patient have not vomited the poisonous matter, which is a characteristic of the disease, and which resembles ricewater, give a table-spoonful of powdered mustard in a tumbler ot cold water, as an emetic. After the vomiting (whether produced by the disease or by the above means), within a few minutes give a wineglass of brandy, with Id grains of powdered capsicum Cayenne pepper stirred up in it. This generally produces almost immediate relief, and within an hour rest, perspiration, and sleep. In a few cases it was found necessary to give a half dose ot the brandy and capsicum of an hour or

more. A second half dose was never required ; but, should it be required, it may be given. No other fluid should be drunk before recovery. To accelerate convalescence, it has been suggested that 15 drops of a mixture of spirit of ammonia and sulphuric ether, in equal parts may be advantageously given three or four times during the following day. The above quantity of brandy and capsicum is for an adult patient suffering a severe attack ; in other cases, two-thirds or half that quantity may sullice, as I have proved by experience."

Heglect of the First Stage of Cholera ! ' It is lamentable," stvs Dr. Drake, a dis- | tinguished American Physician. " to see how many continue to tall victims to the epidemic from neglecting the first stage. 1 repeat the opinion, and would reiterate it with every possible solemnity, that few or none wilold die of the epidemic if the first stages weie attended to. Whenever I have been able to get the history of a fatal case, I have found the patient had one, two, three, or more day's indisposition, chiefly of the stomach and howels, before the spasms and coldness came on Now in thnt forming stage, the malady is ea sily arrested ; when neglected, the patient generally dies. " Could every one who becomes indisposed be induced to take instantly to his bed. and send for a physician, the epidemic would be forthwith deprived of all its horrors The lloman maxim, " resist at the beginning," is not more applicable to any other evil which afflicts mankind than to epidemic cholera." In concluding, 1 must again solemnly and affectionately warn the community that no re liance is to be placed on any plan of treatment that is not entered upon at the very beginning of the disease, and that taking to bed in a warm room at the onset of the complaint and continuing in that situation for several days is indispensable to safety."

Astronomical Clock. þÿ One of the most ingenious pieces ol mechanism ever, perhaps, exhibited in this part of the country, may no w be seen in the Trades' Hall. I lie astronomical clock. made by Mr. Wright, tailor, Aberdeen, is certainly of a new and novel character, and what sorpnses us most is that, after twelve >cuis' study there should be so few wheels, levers, and springs, required to move the machine. This simplicity is howover the greatest compliment thai could be paid lo the ingenuity of ihe inventor ; h>r in nature the all-wise Architect displays his wisdom by making simple means accomplish wonderful operations. The astronomical clock is within un ordinary case, only dillering from that of a common eight day clock in having a glass door, which shows a brass pendulum rod of more than ordinary length, having a fall of 20lbs in weight, and moving slowly, describing a very small arc of a circle. In fiontof this pendulum are two neat iron pullies, bv means of which a weight be keeps the clock motion, in which can ot 7ibs made to go about 14 months before she is run down. As to the dial- plate, we can only give imperfect description an of it. Instead ol 12, it lias '24 hours mai ked upon it þÿ 12 for the

night and 12 for the day þÿ 'I' wo small hands show the days of the month and ihe months of the year. The hour hand, besides indicating the hour of the day. represents the sun, whose time of rising and setting is marked by a moving index on each side of the dial-plate. At the moment of rising, the hour hand, or sun, rising above one index, and at the moment of setting it sinks beneath the other. But here we must rest contented, for we would fail to describe by what means the rising and setting of the moon is shown þÿ "her þÿage her phases, in all their þÿvariations the time of her meridian passage, and her npparent position with respect to the sun. The endearing ties which bind the affections of a community to one who has gained the esteem and confidence of that community, cannot but experience a shock of the most painful nature, when the ruthless hand of deatli interposes, and tears him away, carrying him beyond the pale of human existence. It is an awful visitation ! A visitation which our little community now labours under, in the demise of the respectable, much respected and beloved Chamberlain F. von Sciioltex ; a gentleman whose brilliant ((ualitics shone resplendent through every circle in which he moved. Unaccustomed, as it appeared, to the starckcdness and affected greatness, which mark the character id' some men in high life, this noble individual moved with that case and pleasantness characteristic of a mind unfettered and free. Ilis was not the cold, contemptuous smile, the haughty and domineering manners, which superiors often exercise towards their inferiors, but there was that easy elegance of action about him, which at once called forth the respect, and affection he so much merited and so generally received. And, as haughtiness in high þÿ sed the bitter sarcasms of all, who, more or less, places, receives þÿ however secretly expresare compelled to endure the unfriendly exercise of it : so also must that man who connects a nobleness of mind and feeling with a high rank in life, receive the homage due to his intrinsic worth. Did any one ever see Chamberlain von Si iioi,ten coming along and was not anxious to salute him r

No : all felt it a pleasure to proffer and receive in return, the friendly bow, the kind and openhearted smile, the nod of recognition. Men of all classes and stations, who knew the Chamberlain, whether partially or otherwise, must, with us declare, that he was one of Society's brightest ornament ! Even his enemies, if such he had, could not but honour him. And there are those too, who can bear grateful testimony to his generous and benevolent nature, his willingness to give pecuniary aid to the commonest labourer. Did a porter want money to borrow until he could got work to pay it back ? application was at once made to the Chamberlain ! In a word, our Community has lost its diadem ; his country, a bravo and faithful subject ; his friends, an honorable and agreeable companion ; and the poor, a benefactor and friend. But his name shall spirit is now with " the spirits of just men made iive here : while, it is our lively hope, that his perfect."
West End, December 3rd 1853

From the transactions of the Diet now assembled in Copenhagen we observe, that the Minister of Finance has introduced a bill for doing away with the remission of 25 per ct. on import duties, which since 1841 was allowed on transatlantic produce imported direct to Denmark in vessels having exported cargoes from Denmark ; at the same time modifying the tonnage and light dues in a manner favorable to commerce. The official statement by which the bill has been introduced shows, that, the interest of these Islands in the matter has been considered. The total of charges (including fees, Sound-dues, also the small charges for tonnage tled to the " remission" is now on foreign sugars and light-money) on sugars enti- Rbd. 2 27 sklg. pr. 1001b , on Danish Westindia Sugars Bbd. 1 33 sklg. (excluding fractions;) under the new law it will be Rbd. 2 76 sklg. on the first, and Rbd. 1 73 sklg on the latter. So far the measure is favorable , but it is difficult to foretell, what will be the influence thereof on the

sugars of these Islands in competition with for- I eign sugars (in foreign bottoms) formerly not entitled to "remission." The charges on rum are to remain about the same as before. But more essential advantage will accrue to the Islands, and particularly to St. Croix from the of new ment facilitating the employment such vessels, arrangethat under the present state of law could not be duties; and also removing obstacles, render it almost impracticable for Danish vessels employed for not being entitled to remission which now of ! bound for this Island to take their outward car- goes (coals, machinery, dry goods, d-c.) direct j from England.

A meeting off he members of the.Jamaica Hoard of Immigration was held at the King's House in Spanish Town on Tuesday last the 1st instant. His Excellency the Governor presided on the occasion, and there were present, Robert Russell, William Wright, Henry Franklin, and S. W. Mais, Esquires. Ilis Excellency the Governor, handed to the Hoard a Despatch which he had received from his Grace the Duke of Newcastle, enclosing a letter from the members of the Jamaica Association, pressing for the immediate shipment to this island, of 2,000 immigrants from Madeira, and GOO from the Azores. His Excellency also presented the reply to this letter from the Under Secretary of State for the Colonies, mentioning that in the present state of affairs in the colony, his Grace, the Duke of Newcastle, did not consider it advisable to order a shipment of more than 1,000, the total number of whom will not arrive here, until after 1st May, 1S54. Tenders for conveying the immigrants from Madeira to this island, at the rate of £5 15. for each adult, have been accepted, it seems, by the Land and Emigration Commissioners, and the first shipment will take place in December, and continue monthly, at the rate of 200 per month. Application from the Agents of the ship Clarendon, for payment of the passage money of the Immigrants who lately arrived in this town, was submitted to the Board, and the amount was ordered to be paid.

No Kxcellence without Labor. þÿ Man is created a conscientious and immortal being, lie is endowed with faculties which, if rightly used and appreciated, will exalt him higher as he moves onward in the drama of life, or, it perverted, will sink him as deep as the accessible height he might have attained is high. The love of fame is natural to all, to a greater or less extent ; yet this honor is now innate, it is to be acquired by the effort of our own powers and exertions. And when the mind, that mighty instrument, is wielded with effect, what glorious results crown our success, and encourage us to search out the yet hidden fountains of knowledge; or when the

plicated machinery of of a man is and under the impulse strong at work rous intellect, if attended with like results, what more deserves our praise and admiration than these V Still labor is indispensible, to gain these objects. One may as well attempt to eclipse the sun, or with a lever move the world, as to win excellence without labour. The Oriental philosophers would not likely have achieved such wonderful results, and had

fame had they not entered into their work with heart and hand. Demosthenses would not have overcome such difficulties and shaken all Greece to its very foundations with this startling eloquence, had he not resolved at first to take a de-

maintained that stand with unremitting toil. And even in our own country, the name of Franklin would have been sunk in oblivion, and the great field of his greater work might have been left still unexplored, had he not labored incessantly till he came lo the result lie proclaimed to the world. Thus, it is in all the various works of man, there is no excellence without some degree appli- of cation. If he holds the responsible situation of an officer, he must labor for the benefit of his fellow man, excluding all self-interest if he would gather laurels to deck his pathway, and have his name redound to the latest posterity. It matters not whether he peruse the classic page, or be a student of nature ; in all these there is no excellence without labor.

The vicissitudes and bitter trials of Human Life " The flower that smiles Decay. to day ; Tomorrow dies ; All that we wish to stay ; Tempts and then flies : What is the world's delight ? Lightning that mocks the night Brief even as bright." There are afflictions so agonizing, so overwhelming as to place a barrier to all that the voice of sympathy or friendship would wish to offer, to soothe, were it possible, the anguish of the sufferer. Because, whilst we lament the sad bereavement, reason tells us to control the expressions of profound sorrow, and by doing so, not to over-burden the weight of anguish already too distressing to the breast of an affectionate husband and fapresence ot the desolation caused by the death of a beloved person, the survivors cannot fail to remember, that it is the common lot of humanity, to encounter the severe trials ordained by Providence, to drain the bitter cup, and to bow in silence to the Divine will ! And as no human foresight or power can put aside the stroke of destiny, so are the most exalted in station, or the most humble in life equally doomed to share the bitterness of the draught. Christian fortitude and submission is the path prescribed by God to the mourner under these circumstances ; although, in the first moment of agony which man experiences at the loss of a beloved wife, an affectionate mother, and distinguished member of society, the natural springs of the heart give way, lacerated by anguish,

and the powers of reflection are suspended ; the sufferer not only forgets the necessity of submission, but also his obligations to society, and, moreover, his duty to his children ! Life to him at that crisis is worthless, for he is satisfied to abandon every thing, and in despair to leave the world with the partner, whose endearing presence rendered the measure of felicity to himself and family perfect. Such are the impressions of a mind stricken by a calamity as sudden as heart-rending. Nature however, in her merciful dispensations never allows the hand, the most curious part of the com- I soul to sink, but enables it to regain its empire just at the moment when the sufvigo- I ferer, unable to struggle against the burthen of contending emotions, turns for relief to those around him ; a ray of life Hashes across his mind ; he feels the futility of unreasonable grief; and is made to feel, that however sacred our attachment to the dead, to those who have gone before us, the tribute of the heart, when allowed to extend beyond the limits of reason is incompatible with the their name emblazoned on the scroll of | natural claims of the living who are with us. To mourn is bright, because it is the offering of the wounded mind. Others ! have wept ; have experienced the fragility of human life ; and every thing on which we place our affections, apparently forgetting that passing away is written cided stand against opposition, and i ou the world and all the world contains. This

is an error, the severest of afflictions do not cancel the obligations to God, to society, and to our own family, as we have already alluded. To the contrary, the ties which bind us to existence are the more powerful in regard to the children of the mourner, and when the responsibility of watching over their tender infancy, and providing for their future welfare rests altogether upon him , the warning voice of reason, the influence of parental attachment will be the monitor to whisper " iVace þÿ he still ! With even brow and lips that knows no quivering Go forward to the work thou hast to do, And, in thy heart of hearts, and in its silent depths, Conceal the grief that weighs thy Spirit low ; So shall thy pathway thro' this life be bless'd, Ho shall thy hand strew flow'rs for others, when, None bloom for thee." þÿ þÿ Ht Thomas, 2t>th November 1853.

Christiansted , Friday the 9th December 1853 It is our intention to present to our readers in so far as we can find space in our columns, information of such Judgments, passed in the Courts of this Island, as is deserving of public attention; and as a beginning we communicate the following Judgment passed in Christiansted's Town-Court on the Laborer Jacob Brbndstorff. It will he found to he of interest, as much in respect to the example of brutality of which it treats, happily not often occurring, on the part of one of a married couple; as also in respect to the light which it throws on the principles pursued in our courts of justice, touching evidence in such cases. We understand that Government has caused the Judgment to be appealed to the Upper Court, and it remains to be seen in how far this Tribunal will take the same view of the case as that taken by the Town Judge. JUDGMENT passed in Christiansted's Town Court on the 23d November this year, in Suit No: 23 þÿ 1853, contra Prisoner Jacob Brondstorek. On Sunday the 25th September last, at II o'clock in the night, it was reported to the Police Office in the Centerdistrict, that Caroline Brbndstorff died the same evening at 8 o'clock at the Estate Barren Spot, and that her death was caused by the ill-treatment of her lawful husband. Jarob Brbndstorff, who, at that time, was employed on Estate Kingshill. Jacob Brondstorff was then arrested, and an inquest held the next morning. On the examination of the witnesses it was discovered that the deceased, who had been sick in bed the whole of Satur-

day, about 12 o'clock that same night was found laying on the ground groaning, outside of Daniel's house, which is on the Estate Kingshill and very near thc-one in which Brbndstorff and bis wife lived. Her apparel consisted only of a nightgown. She þÿ could not speak and was carried by was so weak that she Daniel to Ins house, whence she was shortly after taken by Brbndstorff and Daniel to the house of the former. The next day she was removed on a horse by her sister's husband Edward Goosefcldi, and several others, to the Estate Barren Spot, where Gooscfeldt lived. A witness, Jane of Kingshill, has deposed, that she on Saturday evening, at 8 o'clock, was roused out of sleep by BrondstorfPs children who, crying, told her, that Brondstortf had beaten their

mother, and she found, when she went over to Bryndstorfi's house, which is close by, that his wife was laying outside of the house on the ground. Witness brought her into the house and laid her on the bed ; but she rolled from thence on the floor. She did not think that Brbndstorff was drunk. She then went home after having begged Brbndstorff not to ill-treat his wife, and awoke when Daniel called on Brondstortf to carry his wife home. Daniel and Franky his wife, as stated above, live by the side of Brondstorff's house, and have botli deposed, that they heard no noise as they were both asleep, until they were awoke by the cries of Caroline Brbndstorff who laid groaning outside their house at 12 o'clock. Franky deposes that Brbndstorff, when he brought his wife at home, as related above, threw her down on the bed, from which she fell to the floor ; and Daniel declares that every time Brondstorff's wife attempted to speak, he threatened to beat her, in which, however, he prevented him. None of them thought that Brbndstorff was in liquor. Brondstortf's children, of whom the eldest is 11 years old, were present the whole time in the house with their parents, and have given a correspondent statement to the effect that their father beat their mother that evening with a cowskin, and threw tier twice out of the door; besides the hoy Christian Brondstorfl", whose deposition on the whole was given with a high degree of clearness and truth, has deposed, that his father often has beaten, and kicked his

mother. Prisoner, who has acknowledged sometimes to have beaten his wife, has constantly denied to know the least of what had passed that Saturday evening and night, as he insists upon being drunk to that extent as to be out of his senses ; and it is also proved, that he had that, evening received some rum in his house, and that the bottle was afterwards found empty. The witnesses, who saw him the same evening and night, have declared that he did not appear to lie drunk to any great excess ; but be has, notwithstanding this statement, continued his assertion in this respect. The inquest has not thrown further light on the subject, and there lias not been produced any proof that her death lias been caused from ill-treatment. The King's Physician has, however, declared that the ill-treatment, which, according to the examination of witnesses, she has received, may have beet) a concurrent cause of her death. Agreeable to what has been stated, and when it is taken into consideration, that what has been discovered serves only to strengthen the testimony of the children, the prisoner's whole conduct the next morning, I lie expressions he used against his wife and so forth, and that lie rather has asserted not to he able to recollect what had happened, than dared to deny the accusation brought against him, there is certainly a probability near to certainty that Brbndstorff has ill-treated his wife in her sickness, also that he by this ill-treatment has been the concurrent cause of her death ;

but still it does not appear that there has been produced, agreeable to law, sufficient legal proof, as the examined persons, who declare to have been eye-witnesses to the ill-treatment are small children, whose testimony, even if they are, as in the present case, given with a de gree of clearness and certainty, which bears evidence of the truth, yet cannot he considered sufficient to condemn the father. The prisoner, who is 40 years old, and who has not hitherto been punished, will therefore be acquitted of the char-

ges of the prosecutor; the expenses, | to myself. I shewed it to Mr. Hankey, however, of this suit to be defrayed by who requested me to call on him as soon them. The pleading has been legal. Therefore, the follomn sentence is pronounced : The prisoner Jacob Brbndstorffof the Estate kingshill is hereby acquitted of the charges of the prosecutor; however, he will have to defray the expenses of his imprisonment, and to pay all the ex- J those penses of this suit. The sentence to be fulfilled within 15 days after this judgment with ly served, in conformity has been legal- the law.

JUDGMENT passed in the High Court on the 13th October this year, in Suit contra Wit. Brown, of St: Thomas. According to Judgment of 24th Sept. 1852, pronounced by the Town Court of St. Thomas, Win. Brown of that place was sentenced to pay a line of $80, for having committed himself by violent conduct towards the then officiating clergyman of the Episcopal Congregation, Rev. Richards, since dead, on Sunday afternoon the 6th June, during the holding of sunday school in the church. This judgment the Government caused to be appealed to the Upper Court, which by its judgment of the 12th January this year, sentenced Win. Brown to 8 times 48 hours' arrest on bread and water. As Win. Brown desired this judgment to be again appealed, there lias now been given a decisive judgment in the case, bv the High Court in Copenhagen on the 13th October this year, according to which he is sentenced to 10 times 48 hours' arrest on bread and water, besides paying the Advocate's tees $30. Although we are not acquainted with the premisses assumed by the High Court, there is reason to suppose, that this increase of punishment is founded on this fact, that while the Upper Court could not consider Rev. Richards to be entirely free from having given occasion for what transpired (see Ordinance of 4th October 1833 $ 10 1st clause) the High Court has on the other hand, been of opinion that he, Reverend Richards, should be considered as having been attacked without having given the least occasion, (see the same Ordinance 10

We (St. George's Chronicle and Grenada Gazette) have been favoured with the perusal of a private letter received in the last mail from a gentleman in London, from which we have taken the liberty of making the following extract, upon the interesting subject of the Immigration of labourers to this Colony. "I have been introduced to Mr. Thomson Hankey, jun., Agent for Grenada, and we shall be at work for immigration as soon as the Bill, &.c. arrive. He says the grant, or rather the loan, is likely to be extended in amount, as the St. Lucia folks are not requiring the whole, ifany, ot their allotment. I have been introduced also to Mr. Hodge, of the firm of Hyde, Hodge &. Co., the great contractors with Government for the conveyance ot emigrants. They are willing to engage to supply Grenada with Kroomen and other Atricans at £7 a head, so soon as certain restrictions and oppositions ! by the Government Officers at Liberia and Sierra I, cone shall have been remov ed. I asked Mr. Hodge to furnish me with a statement of the obstacles and difficulties that arc in the way, and he did j so þÿ the next day, very clearly, in a letter

as practicable after the arrival of the packet, when, if the Bills and requirements of Government were perfected and forwarded by the Governor-in-Chief, he would be glad to consult with me as to the best means of serving Grenada. It has been suggested by another Gentleman (a West India proprietor) to have a public meeting and the co-operation of interested, desiring to use me in bearing witness to the improved condition of the Africans when removed to the West Indies. Of Grenada 1 can, of course, speak strongly and truly. There is, however, much opposition to the immigration of Africans. President Roberts, of Liberia, is a stumbling-block, and has influenced the Governor of Sierra Leone, who has sent home linfavourble statements to the Colonial Office. Messrs. Hyde, Hodge & Co. are spirited people; and 1 expect that a struggle the sun can be had, in despite the oppo- will be made ere long." sition of Governor McDonald and Presi- If Africans, the " best labourers under ," dent Roberts, the planters of Grenada will need to care little about Chinese and Coolies. But, we very much fear that the Anti-Slavery influence at home, not less than that exercised abroad, overlooking the true state of the case as regards the solicitude with which the condition of the African, as a member of the human family, is sought by all parties to be improved on his introduction amongst us, will be found an insuperable barrier to the promotion of this description of immigration towards the West

Indies. If the advocates for the civilisation of Africa and the Africans would but give themselves the trouble of n ailing over the laws and regulations that are from time to time made for the protection and advancement of the immigrants, or, of ascertaining with how much of rigorous fidelity ail such measures are enforced and carried out in the Colonies, the chances might be favourable as regards us and those whom we take so much interest in training up into industrious and useful members ot' our community. But this they do not generally do. Hence that opposition which they unfortunately believe they are bound conscientiously to set up against every effort to promote the immigration of Africans to the West Indies. þÿ Grenada Gazette.

A difficulty has occurred between the authorities of the Dominican Republic and Mr. T. Elliott, the United States Commercial Agent at the City of San Domingo, in regard to the impressment of several American citizens as soldiers. The Government having paid no attention to Mr. Elliott's repeated protests, he finally wrote to them in the following terms : þÿ " 1 have had the honor to inform you, by my first and second letters, which never were answered, that your Government had pressed some of our American citizens at Porto Plata, who were made soldiers. By this third letter I am sorry to tell you that you will put yourselves into trouble for having insulted my flag in a gross manner, and that my Government will be informed of it immediately, if an answer be not sent without delay." He then received a reply, stating that he must go to the Palace, to the President, vvitli the documents from his Government, to prove that he was the United States Agent. It was supposed that Mr. Elliott would at once proceed to lay i the matter before the United States Government. þÿ New York Tribune.

Paris, Nov. 9. þÿ The increasing irri tation manifested by the Russian Ambassador in Paris as affairs on the Danube become more and more complicated, is very apparent. It is said that he expressed himself very warmly, even angrily, during an interview with the Minister for Foreign Atfiirs, on the general question of the East, but particularly with reference to the articles in one or two of the Ministerial papers, which have re icntly assumed a decidedly hostile tone when speaking of Russia. The Ambassador reminded the Minister how sensitive the French authorities were at the slightest expression of disrespect in them, and how quickly the papers received a warning w hen they ventured to commit themselves, while, as he complained, they were allowed to use disrespectful and offensive language to the Emperor of Russia without check or reprimand. M. Drouyn de Lhuys gave the the circumstances namely, that the only explanation one þÿ could expect undei Government was not responsible for anything that did not appear in its own official organ. The real cause of the angry feeling which breaks out now and then is to be found in the nomination of General Buraguay d'llilliers to the Embas sy at Constantinople. þÿ The Observer.

We are happy to be enabled to lay before our readers, and the voters in Christiansted in particular, the following reply from Mr. Bahneberg to a friend, which will speak for itself; and we have no doubt that the majority of voters in this Jurisdiction will be glad to find that Mr. Bahneberg is willing to resume the post, which, from the circumstances he states, he was compelled to resign. þÿ Christiansted, St. Croix, 1 3th December 1853. þÿ In reply your letter of þÿyesterday s to date, requesting me to state, if I would serve as a member of the Colonial Council, in case of my being re-elected on Friday the 16th instant, I beg to answer, that I have not until now seriously considered the matter, notwithstanding 1 have, as you mention, been asked the question before this by sundry friends. My reason for resigning was, as you are aware, ill health at the time (May last), when it was expected, that the Council would meet in July, by which time I could have no hopes of recovering sufficient strength for going through the business in a creditable manner. As yet I am far from well, and I therefore could have no wish to go in, if a majority of voters had agreed upon another person, as I have been led to believe. If that be not the case, and if I, contrary to my expectation be re-elected, I shall not decline the trust, which I shall endeavour to fulfill as far as in my power. I beg to remain, respectfully, Your most obedient, þÿBAHNEBERG.

From the St. Thomas Times, Nov. 30, 1853. T O K T O L A. Continuation ot'lhe Trial ol' the ISiolcr from our last. þÿsoner C s ounsel You had had a good deal to pri- do Thursday, Nov. 17. Cross-examined by with the lliot ? I have given testimony before the Magistrates against many whom I saw engaged in the Riot. I did say it would give me satisfaction to see many of them hanged, and meant no more than I wished justice to be done ; it would not induce me to say aught against the prisoner what my observation did not warrant me in saying ; was not one of the Rioters, but a loyal subject ; I was a Special Constable but seeing it was hopeless to think of quelling so many with so few Constables, I left the Constables, and came down in the street. I did volunteer to give evidence in thiscase ; I was not examined before the Grand Jury in this case ; it was between 9 and 10 þÿo clock I first saw the prisoner; I was not at that time afraid; I saw many persons on Monday from my gallery ; was oil' and on in the street. The time I allude to as having seen the prisoner was on Tuesday, and not on Monday ; the prisoner was abusing as well as others ; þÿdon k t now what he said, þÿ something abusive of the Magistrates ; did not hear the prisoner abuse the Queen. Re-examined þÿ It was Tuesday ; it was a dreadful day that day I saw the Town on fire ; saw stones thrown by the Rioters at Mr. þÿShow s house, and blood shed ; saw the Rioters attack Mr. Show's house ; I saw a man shot ; saw the town in flames ; from these circumstances I have no hesitation in saying ; it was on the 2nd Augt. ;

made no declaration as regards the prisoner ; my declaration was as regards all who set fire to the houses of innocent and unoffending persons ; I wish justice done ; would not wish to see the prisoner nr any other hung for unjust causes. Mr. Wm. Grown sworn þÿ On Tuesday I saw i large number of persons assembled before Mr. þÿShow shouse ; the prisoner was among them ; they endeavored to force themselves in at the gate ; they all had large sticks (not walking sticks) and knives ; saw the prisoner with a bludgeon, swinging it over his head, and saying he would have St. Domingo ; þÿdon know t what St. Domingo is ; he was very violent ; I saw him between 9 and 10 þÿo clock, and at the time of the firing, and when the fire was set between 12 and 1 ; I saw the prisoner among the crowd, there were immense numbers present. Cross-examined by þÿprisoner s Counsel þÿ I was endeavoring to disperse the Rioters ; I was a Special Constable, under the orders of Mr. Justice Shew ; I had a Fire-lock ; I used it, under orders; it was about between 9 and 10 þÿo clock when they were throwing the stones ; I was stationed in the alley with some others armed ; had not had breakfast ; I breakfast when I can get it ; remained some time in the alley ; þÿdon k t now how long I was looking towards the street, and towards the hill, the stones were coming so fast from both places ; I saw great numbers before the gate, and I do undertake to say I saw the prisoner amongst them ; I saw him also from the win-

dow of the house, when I could get a chance, the stones came so furiously ; a few windows only were open ; 1 went to a window that was open between 12 and l þÿo clock ; I did not quit the bouse from the time went there until I was burned out. I did use my fire lock ; one man was killed, and several were wounded ; the stones were thrown when the man was shot; they then dispersed for a time ; the stones were thrown before the man was shot ; the house was nearly broken down ; the stones were not pebbles ; they were rocks, big rocks, as big as my head some,

4'ns, and some as big as my fist ; they broke down the doors and windows. I went into the house, and could see the man from the place I was standing ; could see 100 or more ; þÿcan tell t how they were all dressed. There were one or two windows open ; I saw the prisoner there. Re-examined þÿ Saw the prisoner amongst the crowd at 9 or 10 ; saw him again between 12 and 1 ; the fire was set about 12 or 1 ; the house was broken open with stones, some large stones, some smaller ; some as big as my fist, and some smaller. Mr. Henry 0. Buntin sworn þÿ Saw the prisoner on the 2nd of August amongst the Rioters ; saw him after the man was shot, trying to urge himself into Mr. þÿShow premises s ; he might have been there before, but I did not see him. Mr. S. Bryan, Colonial Treasurer, sworn þÿ Saw the prisoner at the Bar amongst the Rioters, first at 10 þÿo clock,again about 2 þÿo clock ; when the fire was set heard the prisoner distinctly say þÿ burn them to þÿhell. A cry of fire, and a volley of stones were simultaneous. I know Mr. Justice Shew; he read the Riot Act more than once from the window, and advised the people to go away. I saw the prisoner subsequently ; I got out of the house when it was burning, with a double-barrelled gun of Mr. þÿShew in s my hand ; this man pursued me ; he took up a brick to throw at me ; I pointed my gun at him ; he ran away through the bushes. I then made off, and he threw the brick at me, and subsequently a second one. There were in the street upwards of

1000 persons ; þÿcan undertake t to say what color shirt this man had on. I was alarmed ; was looking through the window, and persuading them to disperse, when I was struck by a stone. 1 know the prisoner ; he has worked for me. Sophia Amoy sworn þÿ Saw7 the prisoner on 2nd of August ; saw him between 9 and 10 pass my door with a large stick, going down with about 1000 persons ; they had knives and sticks and bills, and I saw one with a pistol. I saw him before the fire and after the fire, at one time on the hill throwing stones ; he was very violent þÿ a sort of leader amongst them. Cross-examined þÿ Saw the faces of the mob ; many of the faces I knew ; I saw all the faces. Mr. Isaacs, the þÿQueen C s ouusel, summed up. The learned Counsel for the defence addressed the Jury. The learned gentleman contended that the evidence was insufficient to support the Indictment ; it was not conclusive that the prisoner remained one hour with the Rioters after the Proclamation was read. To come to this conclusion, and acquit the prisoner, it was by no means necessary the Jury should disbelieve the testimony of the respectable witnesses who had been on the floor, but in the absence of having spoken to any act committed by the prisoner, of their having held converse with him ; there was a possibility of their having been mistaken as to the identity of the prisoner; before the Jury would be justified in returning a verdict of þÿ þÿGuilty, it must believe that the prisoner was the man spoken of

and no other. The learned gentleman then read from a legal text-book some cases of mistaken identity, and argued therefrom the possibility of all these witnesses being mistaken. Mr. þÿBryan s view from a window was necessarily imperfect. The learned gentleman then endeavored to show that Felix Francis was also mistaken ; that he had stated he knew Andrew, the prisoner, because he was heside a man whom lie did not know. The question of withdrawing the Troops from the West Indies, so much harped upon since the Free-Traders came into power in the State, is now, according to the rumour in certain quarters, on the eve of being practically carried out. But, for our own part, we do not think it can be in contemplation immediately to introduce any change in the distribution of the colonial garrisons. By the very last mail from England, we find the periodical reliefs and exchanges of troops announced in the usual way. The 4 1st, 44th, 47th, and 49th regiments have been ordered to proceed from Malta, and the 30t h regiment from Gibraltar, to the West Indies and Bermuda; relieving the 69th which goes to New Brunswick, the 67th, which goes to Canada,

and the 10th, 36th, and 56th, which return to the United Kingdom; the 71st, from Canada, and the 72nd from New Brunswick, will also return to the United Kingdom. 'l'he Windward and Leeward command, which embraces Barbados, British Guiana. Trinidad, Tobago, Grenada, St Lucia, St. Vincent, Dominica, Antigua, Montserrat, Nevis. St. Kitts and Tortola, it is estimated, costs £210.000 a-year and Jamaica £40,000 þÿ making £250,000 for the armv, with £20- 000 for the navy, £14.000 for governors, and £9,000 for bishops þÿ in all £293,000 as the the total expense borne annually by England for these colonies. This outlay our þÿ liberal financiers grudge to incur any longer; and they allege that the colonies þÿ are useless and a burthen to the mother-country therefore. the army which costs so much, they say, must be withdiawn; and the useless and burthensome batch of colonies, if requiring military or naval defence or protection, must themselves find the means of procuring and maintaining it. When the West Indies weie in more prosperous circumstances, the Parent Government did not hesitate to provide them with all necessary military protection; but, strange to say, now that they can least afiord it, and now that the effects of a vast social revolution must naturally enhance the necessity for a protective force, they are to be abandoned to their own resources Whilst we are reproached with entailing so large an outlay on the Home Government, and ate said to be burthensome and useless, it is re-

markable that no credit whatever is given for the duly we pay on the produce which our industry sends home, nor the amount ol it, nor the value ol English goods of which we are large consumers. It is not taken into account that the colonies named above ship every year about 160,000 tons of sugar, on which, tor a long series of years, they paid 27s. a cwt., afterwards 24s , then l ls., then down to 10s. Fair and faithful calculations like the following, which we lake from a very clear-headed authority, go tor nothing with our " liberal" repudiators : þÿ 100,000 tons sugar, at 10s. duty. give £1,000,000 I)utv on rum and molasses, one tourtli 400,000 On coffee and other exports 700,000 2,100,000 Value of produce independently of the þÿduty. Taking the sugar at 40s., and deducting the 10s. duty, and the expense of cultivation 10s. more, 20s. clear are left for England, for its food, the employment of its mercantile navy, its merchants, its docks, its ware- houses, &c. - -- -- -- -- -- -- 4,200,000 Value ot goods from England in return lor the produce sent home ------ 3,200,000

£9,500,000 Yet the protection by the Troops, which cost only £250,000 is to be withdraw!) ; and these colonies, though giving the mothercountry a clear gain, as shewn above, ol between nine and ten millions sterling annually, are deemed þÿ a useless burthen þÿ! Notwithstanding the rumoured approach, however, of this groat slioke ol economy, the real nature of the plan to be acted upon remains still unexplainen to us; and it is not known whether the determination is to withdraw the forces entirely, or only to reduce their numbers, or concentrate them in some few chosen localities. It is not improbable, wo think, that the latter arrangement will be the one adopted, as we have seen it suggested that þÿ a judicious þÿconcentration of the troops on whai may be considered the best and most impoiunt of our military positions in the

colonics, should be one of the objects aimed at, in preference to the present wide-spread dispersion of them. The existing system has been, in influential quarters, ptonounced to be vicious, in respect to the weak and attenuated detachments which it distributes of an army, and the creation it makes of a number of costly and inefficient establishments, as well as its alleged tendency to destroy morale and discipline ; and it has been contended, too, that the police purposes for which our soldiers are scattered amongst the islands, can be met now-a-days by the increased facility afforded of transport by the power of steam, whereby any required portions of troops could with celerity and certainty be moved to the scene of any threatened disturbance. In the event of this being the arrangement taken, the four regiments of infantrv and four companies of artillery (about 3,000 men) now distributed amongst the , thirteen stations in the Windward and Leeward Command, would fie concentrated on some three or four of those colonies possessing the best harbours and affording the best military positions þÿ such as Barbados, '1 þÿrim dad, Antigua, Grenada, and St. Lucia ; and the other islands would, in that case, be left to take care of themselves by means of a militia, the reorganization of which, it is understood. has recently been recommended and urged by the Home Government.

The long circulated rumour of withdrawing the Troops from the smaller islands and concentrating them at Barbados, Trinidad and Antigua, seems to have more truth iu it than was at first supposed ; as it is confidently stated that this arrangement will take place in March or April next, when the annual reliefs of regiment take place. TOBAGO. ( From the Chronicle.) We linve been politely favoured by a gentleman, with the perusal of a letter from a friend of bis in Madeira, in which some interesting information is conveyed, relative to Immigration from that Island. It appears that there is no difficulty at present in procuring Portuguese labourers if proper means he adopted. Numbers of them still continue going to Demerara, notwithstanding the mortality among their countrymen there, arising from yellow fever. It is stated in the letter that they would sign an agreement for three years at the customary rate of wages to come to this Island, consequently proprietors possess a favorable opportunity of adding to the labouring strength on their estates, at present so much required. As we understand the letter referred to, will soon he published, it is unnecessary that we should do more than briefly allude to it at present.

New Revolving Rifles. þÿ We have had the pleasure of examining a most interesting and valuable improvement in repeating firearms, known as þÿ Porter patent s þÿrifle. It may be discharged nine limes without intermission and loaded nearly as fast as charges can be poured from a powdeiflask. Its construction and operation are also beautiful ly simple and exceedingly solid and effective. A solid wheel or cylinder, 3 to 3j inches in diameter, and three-fourths of an inch thick, is fitted vertically in the breech, producing equal above and below, revolving on journals, and presenting its face closely to the end of the barrel, which fits it nicely and is thereby closed. The face of this cylinder is perforated with nine chambers an inch deep, each corresponding to the bore ot the barrel, and each in turn brought into position by the barrel and form part of it. These, of course, revolution of the cylinder, so as to match the j ' may all be charged at once. The cylinder rests firmly on its journals, against the action of the discharge, and is also supported at its circumference by the iron portion ol the breach iu which it revolves. Each chamber has a touchhole communicating with the centre of the charge and opening on the right side of the cylinder, covered when in position by the end of the cap, which is struck internally and horizontally by a nippleshaped hammer. The lock, a very simple piece of mechanism, is fixed at one end to the barrel bv a hinge, closing and clasped upon the side

of the cylinder, when ready for use, but otherwise opening, and allowing the cylinder to be taken out and charged, or exchanged for another, at pleasure. To it is attached a i cap-box, accommodating thirty caps and presenting one at the touchhole of each chamber as it comes into place. In the military gun, however, the ordinary nipple receiving the cap is connected with each chamber. The trigger guard is also a lever, turning the cylinder precisely one slop at each moment, and cocking the hammer at the same time. Three fingers of the right hand pass naturally through a loop in this guard, and by a slight motion downward and hack, the cylinder is turned the proper distance as often as the I hand can move. This motion, and the pres- j sure of the trigger alternately, are all that is necessary to discharge the piece, which may easily be done nine limes in as many seconds The ball can be driven through a 4 inch j plank at 25 þÿyards. From the Observer, January 15, 1854. THE TURCO-RUSSI AN WAR. NOTE OF THE FOUR POWERS. The undersigned ambassador of her Britannic Majesty, in accordance with the representatives of Fiance, Austria, and Prussia, has the honour to make known to the Sublime Porte that the Governments of the four Powers, having still reason to believe thai his Majesty the Emperor of Russia does not regard the thread of negotiations as broken by the declaration of war, and by the events the consequence thereof; and knowing, moreover, according to the proposed declarations of his Imperial Majesty, that he desires only to behold assured a perfect equality of rights and immunities octroyed by his Majesty the Sultan and his glorious ancestors to the Christian communities, subjects of the Sublime Porte; on its part, the Sublime Porte responding to those declarations by that which it made itself to regard it as concerning its honour to continue to maintain t he said rights and immunities, and to be still disposed to put an end to the difference arising between the two Powers ; The negotiation to be followed shall be based upon : þÿ " 1 The most speedy evacuation possible of the principalities. " 2 The renewal (renouvellement) of ancient treaties. " 3. The communication of the firmans relative to the spiritual privileges octroyed by the Sublime Porte to all its subjects not Mussulmen, which communication, made to the Powers, should be accompanied by suitable assurances given to each of them, The arrangement already made to complete the agreement (I'accord) relative to the

holy places and to the religious establishments of Jerusalem shall be definitively adopted. " This arrangement concerns the erection of a church and the establishment of a Russian hospital at Jerusalem. " The Sublime Porte shall declare to the representatives that it is ready to name a plenipotentiary to establish an armistice, and to negotiate on the above-mentioned bases, with the concurrence of the Powers, and in a neutral town to be agreed upon between them " The declarations made by the Powers in the preamble of the treaty of July 13, 1841, shall be formally confirmed by those same Powers in the interest of the independence and integrity of the Ottoman Empire, and in that of the equilibrium of Europe (et de celui du concert Kuropien). " The Sublime Porte shall declare (dectarerait) on its part in the snme interest its firm resolution to develope more efficaciously its administrative system, and those internal reforms of a nature to satisfy the wants and the just expectations of its subjects of all classes (Signed) " Stratfoud de Redcliffe, " Bahaguay d'Hilliers, " L. de Wtr.DENBttirCK, " B. de Bruck. " Pera, Dec. 13, 1853. The note, it will be seen, assumes throughout that the whole quarrel between the Czar and the Porte relates to religious differences. Up to its date I' ranee arid England had denied what is thus assumed, and had shown the assumption to be false. By what folly or meanness are they induced now to contradict their former statements and admit the falsehood of
the Czar ?

The Heraldo of Madrid, of the 22nd, states that a deputation of senators and deputies of the liberal party had waited on the Minister of Justice, to request that a certain degree of liberty should be allowed to the periodical press, and that the newspapers should be protected from sudden seizures and editors from arrest by the local authorities. The minister said that it was impossible for the cabinet to take the matter into consideration until the President of the Council should be better. A letter says that the President was getting better, and that he had been able to transact business. AVc have advices from Madrid to the 2Sth ult. A decree in the Gazette enacts that the establishment of the metrical system, which was to have come into operation, this year, shall be postponed to 1855. The Marquis de Turgot was going on well, although his wound continued to cause great pain. The materiel purchased in England for a line of telegraphs from Madrid to Irun had arrived. The line is to pass by Saragossa, and is to be placed in communication with the French lines. It is expected that it will be completed in four or five months. A letter says that the Queen continued in good health, and drove out daily ; her medical attendants did not think her confinement would take place for some days. CONSTANTINOPLE, Dec. 31. PERFIDY OF THE NORTHERN POWERS. The Prussian and Austrian Ambassadors at Constantinople were "in a state of consternation" when the orders were received for the combined fleets to enter the Black Sea. Both ambassadors had protested against that measure. A communication was received from Vienna, expressing the "surprise" occasioned by two Powers taking it upon themselves to solve a question in the manner mentioned (namely, by the orders given to the fleets), which had been taken into consideration by the Four Powers, with a view to an arrangement. Great joy was felt at Constantinople when it was known that the fleets had really received orders to protect the Turkish convoys, and, of course, to prevent any collision between the Russian and Turkish navy. Still the fleets have not stirred from their anchorage, with the exception of four steam frigates, which have shifted their quarters to the lighthouse, at the embouchure of the Euxine into the Dardanelles.

From the Observer, January 15, 1854. GREAT FIRE AT NEW YORK. DESTRUCTION OF THE SHIP GREAT REPUBLIC. On the 2tilh ult., a fire broke out in New York, which destroyed upwards of a million dollars' worth of property. The conflagration first commenced in Front-street, and extended on both sides. Some of the sparks from the burning buildings were blown into the sails of the colossal ship Great Republic, which was lying in an adjacent dock, nearly ready to sail for Liverpool, and, in a very short period, she was one mass of flames. The burning materials then communicated to the packet-ship Joseph Walker, and the celebrated clipper White Squall. The three ships, notwithstanding energetic endeavours to save them, were totally destroyed. The Great Republic, valued at 300,000 dollars, was insured for 180,000 dollars ; the cargo valued at the same amount as the vessel, was insured for 275.000 dollars. The Joseph Walker, valued at 90,000 dollars, was insured for the full amount ; the cargo valued at 40 000 dollars, was uninsured. The White Squall was fully insured for 80,000 dollars Many vessels had narrow escapes from sharing the fate of the Great Republic. The De Witt Clinton was cut adrift, and escaped the flames, as did likewise the clipper Whirlwind, not. however, before she had some part of her rigging destroyed The Herald thus describes the conflagration : þÿ " While the fire was raging in Front-street the sparks were so thick in the vicinity as to assume the appearance of a shower of fire. The streets and docks along the East River were literally

alive with burning coals. The pier at the foot of Dover-street was at one time covered to the depth of some inches with fire, and the rigging and masts of the numerous vessels lying in the stream were completely enveloped in flying sparks." The sails of the Great Republic were partially unfurled, preparatory to her departure on her first voyage, and, in consequence of the extraordinary height of the mast, the engines produced little effect at first. Hose Companies Nos. 19 and 31 were among the first to get near the vessel. The companies, startled by the explosion of the ship's hatches, were somewhat apprehensive of the presence of powder on board, but being assured by Capt. M Kay that there was no danger, they began to work with a will. The noise of the explosion is attributed to the escape of confined steam from the interior. The flames, which had begun to be under control when the foremost fell, burst out afresh instantly, and raged with uncontrollable fury. The vessel was now a perfect wreck, being soon one mass of flames abaft the mainmast. The loss by the destruction of the Great Republic and cargo will probably reach the amount of 700,000 dollars. The sight presented was truly sublime. The rigging was enveloped in flames from the topmast to the deck, and as they were swayed from side to side, threw out huge tongues of fire. The streets were crowded with spectators, although a storm raged with violence, and the cold was so great that the water, as it fell, froze on the
side of the burning vessel. The air was filled with sparks from the burning houses. So violent was the wind that some buildings along the docks were

ATI8» threatened, and the wonder is, not that so much property was destroyed, but that the loss has not been greater The air was filled with sparks and burning fragments. At one moment a dense cloud of black smoke would sweep down upon the spectators, shutting out of view the burning ships, and, on this rolling away, the terrific sight would break most vividly upon them. The foremost of the Great Republic first went by the board, falling with a terrible crash, and threatening the lives of the firemen standing on the side of the vessel. The mainmast then fell across the pier into the dock, capsizing a small boat, and knocking four men, its occupants, into the water. They were fortunately saved, The Joseph Walker was set fire to by sparks from the burning buildings in Front-street, nearly at the same time with the Great Republic. Strange to say, the Constellation, which lay at her bows, escaped without a single spar being scorched. The Joseph Walker was a Liverpool packet ship, owned by Messrs. Thompson and Nephew, not more than two years old, and fully insured in the offices in New York. She had in her cargo 500 barrels of rosin. The burning brands from the Great Republic set fire to the White Squall. By great exertions the White Squall was cut adrift, and floated off towards getic the fire would have Brooklyn in such a mass of flame that it was totally impossible to attempt to scuttle her. Thousands of anxious spectators awaited her arrival in Brooklyn. About half-past three in the morning she eame against the wooden

wharf of the Brooklyn Gas Company's Works, when she was made fast and deluged with water; but, as another fire happened to be then raging in Brooklyn, the force of the firemen was divided. However, by nine o'clock I Wednesday morning, the flames were overcome, the vessel being then a total wreck. The aggregate loss by these fires is but little shoit of 1,000,000 dollars. þÿ »ooo«- þÿ POPULAR OUTBREAK IN THE TURKISH CAPITAL. CONSTANTINOPLE, Dec. 23. " Never since the commencement of the present question pending between Turkey and Russia has there been a more favourable prospect for the arrangement of the differences than at present. The note has been presented to the Sultan's Government by the representatives of the four Powets; and the Divan has accepted it. The armistice is the fundamental condition. But never has Constantinople presented a more serious and dangerous aspect. The day before yesterday the whole of this city was in a state of great alarm. On that day the Softas (students of divinity), together with a considerable mob, assembled in different parts of the vast city þÿ especially round the mosque of the Sultan Mehemet, and that of Sheik Zade. The houses of prayer were closed, and a movement commenced which bid fair to become very dangerous. The shops and warehouses at Constantinople were closed. The idea gained ground that the Turkish population meditated an attack upon the Christians, which, as may well be imagined, caused intense anxiety. The ambassadors of the dif-

ferent Powers sent word to their respective subjects, and to all the merchants and other persons who have warehouses within the capital, and who are in the habit of spending the greater portion of the day there, to be on their guard, and to return to the Christian

suburbs. This intimation was not lost upon them, and they hurried across the great bridge that connects the suburbs with the capital, in double-quick time. It is astonishing how soon news spreads, and especially that of an ominous character þÿ how it swells gradually, and increases in import as it passes from mouth to mouth. On Wednesday morning scarcely anybody knew anything of what was going on. By mid-day nobody spoke of anything else. The alarm in this instance, however, was not unfounded, and it may be termed a very ugly occurrence. I dare say, that by the time this reaches you, the British and French public will have been electrified by the fearful news of a revolution at Constantinople. a massacre of the Christians, and God knows what besides. There have been tumults at Constantinople ; but that is all. Not a shot has been fired. The heads of the movement have all been arrested ; 400 Softas arc at this moment in the hands of the Government. The whole affair has been nipped in the bud. From good information which I have obtained on the subject, I feel convinced that the origin of this outbreak was not directed against the Christians, but against the pashas, who signed the note þÿ against the party that advocates peace. No doubt, had enermeasures not been adopted the first in instance, spread, and, once well lit, there is no knowing where it would have slopped, or what might have happened. Reschid I'asha, the Tuikish Minister of Foreign Affairs, was greatly alarmed, and start-

ed off immediately, together with his sons, for the Sulian's palace. He has been nicknamed Giaour I'asha. A person of my acquaintance, who was at Constantinople on saw him get into his carriage, as pale as death. This gentleman was himself pelted with stones, and had to make off as fast as his horse could carry him. Since then matters have cooled down a little, and many Europeans have been to Stamboul without being molested It would, however, by no means be safe to take a ramble there alone, and 1 do not think any person who knows what feeling is abroad would venture to do so. The Turkish population have got it into their heads that an ignominious peace has been stipulated, and that they are to be robbed of their privileges, for the benefit of the Christians, and to the detriment of the Mahomedan faith. Ever since the late disastrous affair at Sinope they have been much irritated. They feel disappointed that the British and French fleets did not at once proceed to the Black Sea, and take an active part against the Russians. It is very fortunate that the combined squadrons ate in the Bosphorus. Were these protective forces not near at hand, many a man who now has a smirk on his face would be drawing a long breath. Even as it is, the Christian subjects of the Porte are in great fear and trembling."
