We copy from the Barbados Liberal of the 21st ult. the following: þÿ " The Barbadian cannot believe " that the inundation ofsea water and its lodgement on the Island, could have produced the fatal epidemic" of Cholera in the island of St. Thomas, as has been surmised by the Government Medical Inspector. Our contemporary remembers instances of similar inundations here, that were not attended with any such consequences; but he forgets the conditions upon which the lodgement of sea water might depend for its malignant character, which, it can very well be understood, may have been present in the one case and not in the others. " Sea water in its pure state is generally innocuous. Left upon the earth in that state to evaporate, the pure water would be carried off, and the residi im would consist of a wholesome salt with certain quantities of mineral substances not calculated to affect health by their exhalations. But when sea water is mixed up with fresh water, and especially when animal or vegetable matter iti process of decomposition enters into the commixture, it rapidly undergoes those chemical changes which are popularly known under the name of "corruption" þÿ which is, in fact, but a general decomposition þÿ anil throws off exhalations highly detrimental to animal, and in some circumstances even to vegetable life. " Now, this is precisely what might be inferred, without any stretch of imagination, or the least strain upon the premises, to have been the case in St.

Thomas. We all know that cane fields are commonly highly manured, and con- I tain therefore both animal and vegetable P matter in a state of decomposition. And sea water lodging upon those fields would necessarily take up this decomposing matter, and be rendered by it corrupt and deleterious, and the more readily if assisted by rain. Nor is this all in the St. Thomas' case ; for although disease would very probably be the result of inhaling the poisonous exhalations from this source, it does not follow, as of course, that that disease should he Cholera. But in the case before us there was another and important condition that would probably give it tbat particular tendency. We mean the peculiar susceptibility at the moment to Cholera. What this is, whence it proceeds, or on what it depends, is yet a mystery to all, the learned and unlearned alike, and may forever remain so. But Cholera existed in the neighbourhood of St. Thomas, as it exists at this time in our own neighbourhood þÿ hundreds of miles apart, but not the less in the neighbourhood, radiating its malign influence; and the tendency of certain morbific causes to produce this particular disease is immensely greater, in consequence, than at other times. The truth is, that in all these colonies, from the near approach of Cholera, there is vastly more danger from foul exhalations, and the like, at the present time, than ordinarily; and no argument can he legitimately drawn from past immunity, under essentially
different circumstances to favour the idea of a like immunity now. And, for this reason, we think it advisable "that"

sy the collection of wnter at ' Merrv-wing II. ill,' the residence of Mr. George Kve- 1 v 1 1 , " si ii offensive odour which," our contemporary tells tts, " sometimes annoys the tinveller along that road," should he speedily looked after hy the local authorities of the parish (Christ Church), and the nuisance abated, notwithstanding the reputed healthiness of the neighbourhood at other times. That stink does riot promote the healthiness under any circumstances, and just now might offer the same sort of inducement to Cholera, which the opening up of a rich pasture would offer to a flock of plovers in the Bird season. » We had intended a few words, in conclusion, on our contemporary's repudiation of that attention to "second causes" for the origin of disease, which, to his view, militates against a proper sense of the Divine Government hy the Almighty. But we content ourselves, at present, with simply quoting his own concluding remark, which, however irreconcilable with such general repudiation of "second causes," exactly meets our case. " Earnestly, indeed, should we set about," he says, "using all human means to avert or mitigate the evil, hut with an humble dependence on Ilim to bless our exertions, or to prepare our minds to meet the visitation with patience and resignation." The most earnest hunter after second causes could not say more in their favour, or say it better. The only difference between such a one and our contemporary is, that the former sets about his exertions

thoughtfully, and in the most effective manner, by first endeavouring to ascertain in what direction they are to he turned, and to what immediate effect. In other words, both are for an earnest appliance of " human means" to stay the evil; but whilst one looks about to find the proper "means to be applied in the case, the other avails himself of the discovery, hut, at the same time, ensures the discoverer for presumed impiety in the search." þÿ Ibid. v V <e- If it bo true that Captain Elliot will be our future Governor, it is most likely that the Colonial M inister intends to give us a Representative Government, as, if report may be believed, the Gallant Capt. is a man of liberal principles. Rut, whoever may be Governor, and whatever may be the disposition of the Ministry, we think our fellow-colonists ought to bestir themselves to make their voice again heard in support of their reasonable demands. We do not think that any future Governor could do us more harm, as a trading community, than Lord Harris has done ; and therefore we do not think that the Island can be absolutely ruined : but we want, not to be stationary, but to progress according to the measure of our capabilities: and we ask our readers to consider whether in these days any country, despotically ruled, progresses ? In do former ages an enlightened despotic ruler might much, but in this century the general advancement of the world is too rapid ; the collision and energy of many minds are requisite to keep pace with it ;

such cannot be found in Legislative Councils composed of nominees overborne or fettered as can is the case with our government. England scarcely deny us the privileges which she is granting to Jamaica; the theory of Representative Government has been much improved by the additional knowledge gained by the working of it in Canada and other Colonies within a few years past : some of the dangers dreaded have been proved to be chimerical, others have been averted by the modifications which trial and experience have dictated. With the power of England to procure order, and the abilities of her liberal statesmen to interpose and direct us in the right way, we cannot see what evils could arise even from the natural errors of men new to legislative functions. And wo exhort our fellow-colonists not to let pass this opportunity of re-asserting their rights. þÿ San Fernando Gazette, Jan. 27.
LONDON, THURSDAY, JANUARY 5, 1854. Some doubts having been expressed as to the conduct the Northern Courts ofSwcden and Den-

D 'Ji t> 'I X A T i S mark may think fit to adopt in the event of an extension of the hostilities which have commenced on the Danube and the Black Sea, those Powers have recently determined to establish a strict union of their policy, and a formal declaration of their intentions has just been addressed by their Ministers, in identical terms, to all the Cabinets of Europe. Whatever may be the result of the differences which have occurred between Russia and Turkey, and which threaten to extend to the maritime Powers, Sweden and Denmavk are desirous of maintaining their friendly relations with all the States now at amity with them, and, accordingly, they propose to observe in the contest which may now be impending over the world a strict neutrality, by abstaining from every direct or indirect measure calculated to favour or assist cither of the contending parties. For this purpose they propose to admit, without distinction, to their ports the merchant vessels and vessels of war belonging to the belligerents on either side, with the sole exception of privateers, which are to be prohibited from entering Swedish and Danish harbours. The only exception to this free access in the case of Denmark is the port of Chri.-tianso, which is used as a State prison ; and in the ease of Sweden, foreign vessels of war are not to enter the principal harbours within the line of certain forts. They further propose to concede to both parties full liberty of trading and ohtaiuing supplies, with the exception of articles contraband of

war ; but they lay it down as a rule of their neutrality that, except under pressure of weather, no maritime prizes are to be taken in, condemned, or sold in their ports, or in their Courts of Admiralty. Lastly, they assert for themselves the right to carry on their own mercantile and other relations with the States which may be engaged in this war, subject to existing laws, and, of course, to such conditions as the state of war may impose. As several months must still elapse before the Baltic ports are open either to the prosecution of trade or to operations of war, the Northern Courts might, without practical inconvenience to navigation, have deferred this declaration some time longer, or till war between the maritime Powers is actually commenced. But they have taken a more politic as well as a more decided course, and this announcement of neutrality was the proper answer for them to give to the imputation of Russian iufluence. Confused and exaggerated statements of the position of these Governments towards Russia were already current, and had obtained circulation in the west of Europe. But later information from Sweden contradicts the statement that Russia had made any direct attempt to obtain from the Baltic States a measure of so hostile a character as the closing of their ports agai:;st French or English vessels in the event of war, and in the meantime these Governments were engaged in a negotiation of which the maritime Powers of Western Europe have no right to

complain. The idea of an armed neutrality has also been mentioned, probably from some indistinct reminiscence of the maritime convention concluded by the Baltic States with Russia in 1780 ; but nothing of the kind is to be found in the present declaration. The neutrality of these States means their independence, and it secures us against the only danger we could apprehend in the Baltic from the nscendancy Russia might havo attempted to exercise in ports not belonging to her empire. The Emperor Nicholas will find that, under these present circumstances, the alliance of the Baltic States altogether fails him ; and, if he should make any attempt to urge them to depart from the lino of policy they have adopted, wo havo no doubt that the spirit of the people and the interests of tho two Crowns would lead them to resist every attempt at foreign dictation. It is a mistake to suppose that the Scandinavian kingdoms are under Russian influence ; and the promptitude with which they have declared themselves on this occasion is a distinct refu-

tation of the charge sometimes brought against them. Sweden is too near St. Petersburg, and has already lost too much important territory on the side of the Russian frontier, to render her a very confiding neighbour ; and the policy of both the Courts is, very wisely, to make the Baltic a free and open sea, both in peace and in war

From JVilmer and Smith's European Times, January 16, 1854. C 81 I ft A. PROGRESS OF the rebellion. re-capturb of amoy, and execution of 1000 of the rebels. Hong Kong, Nov 27. þÿ The local news of this place is of the usual dull character, and is of trifling interest, but the intelligence which the present mail conveys to Europe is important in relation to the progress of the rebellion, which is fast breaking up the Chinese Empire. The Health of Hong Kong is somewhat unfavorable, owing to the late hot sultry weather, and has been marked by increase to the sick list of the garrison. Civilians, too, have felt the effects of the high temperature. Of the garrison no less than 113 are in hospital, and of this number 75 belong to the 59th Regiment. Eever, bowel, and chest complaints have been and are still prevalent, and four deaths have taken place in the garrison since the middle of the month. About seventy invalids will shortly proceed home, and the whole of the Ceylon Rifle Regiment is in orders to return to Ceylon, leaving the military strength of the garrison very low. At Canton, and in its immediate vicinity, all was quiet. The number of executions for political offences affords clear evidence that the Imperial authorities are anxious to strike terror into the minds of all classes of the population From Shanghai advices have been received to the 19th instant. The belligerents keep up a desultory warfare with little or no effect, and the struggle is aided and prolonged by some injudicious foreigners, who, for the profit attaching to

the sale, do not hesitate to furnish the imperialists and insurgents with arms and ammunition. But for the supplies so furnished it is probable that both parties would quietly endeavour each to tire out and exhaust the patience of the other, instead of which they are tempted to struggle for mastery without the probability of accomplishing anything. It would also appear that the Imperialists, having heard that some guns were about to be removed from a foreign hong to the head-quarters of the rebels, endeavoured to prevent the coolies carrying the guns away ; and it would also seem that these imperialists had provided materials which induced the foreign community to believe that they designed to burn down their houses. The consequence was a general turn out of all the foreign residents, aided by armed parties from the shipsof-war. With Mr. Wade, the Eritish Vice-Consul, at their head, the foreign residents drove the Imperialists from their settlement, although not without exchanging shots, in which some six or seven of the Imperialists were wounded. On the following day Messrs. Wade and Meadows were sent by the British Consul with a despatch to Keih, the judge, to demand an explanation ; that functionary stated that the imperial soldiers were under the general, and that strict orders had been given them not to enter the British limits. On the 18th November Keih informed the British consul that on their return to camp the imperialists had reported that they were driven back by

rebels dressed up in foreign clothes. The British consul has issued a notification relative to the attack, in which he deplores the loss of life that ensued, and congratulates the foreign community that no worse mischief ensued. The consul enjoins forbearance, and deprecates the furnishing of military supplies to the belligerents as subversive of the line of policy, strict neutrality, which the British government had intimated its intention to pursue. The ex-Taoutac has been exerting himself to retake the city, but failed, after a most desperate attempt by sea and land. Early on the morning of the 9th November, the ex- Taoutae despatched spies through the city to report that he proposed to quit for Chin-Keang- Foo, and when his fleet got under weigh, the report was deemed well founded. The wily mandarin, after a little manoeuvring, suddenly sailed right for the city, and opened a brisk fire upon the insurgents' batteries, which could not be returned from the latter without firing into the neutral fleet. Shortly after the insurgents commenced a canonade, doing much damage to the Taeniae's fleet The second division attacked the square-rigged vessels Glonlyon and Snipe, belonging to the insurgents, and obtained possession of them, not by boarding, but by throwing on board a shower of stink pots ; the smoke and flames wore such that the crew were compelled to jump overboard, and endeavoured by swimming to reaon the shore ; the boats of the Taoutae attacked the

poor wretches in tho water, and speared every one that appeared above water. The imperialists, assisted by several foreigners in the Taoutae's fleet, made repeated attempts to capture the forts, but were bravely repulsed. After this, the imperial-

3 JT A T I 3, ists' boats proceeded along tho shore and set fire to one of the suburbs, which destroyed about 1,500 houses and an immense amount of property belonging to the rich merchants and shopkeepers in the neighbourhood. The parties employed in this work of wanton destruction consisted of the west coast pirates, who pillaged the district before they set fire to the dwellings, and carried off' a large amount of treasure, opium, provisions, SfC. Simultaneously with the naval attack an attempt was made to carry the city on the land side, where 3,000 imperialists advanced for the purpose of taking the city by surprise. The sentinels kept concealed until the advanced post, finding all quiet, bolaly scaled the walls ; as soon as the first three ascended the ramparts their heads were instantly cut off, and immediately a brisk fire was opened along the whole line, which forced a quick retreat. The imperialists returned to their camp in confusion, with many of their numbers killed and wounded. In the naval and land engagements it is estimated that 300 of the imperialists lost their lives. From Amoy the most melancholy accounts have been received, involving an amount of bloodshed that is calculated to strike terror into the hardest heart, and with any other people than Chinese would induce a reaction and a cry of vengeance on the author of such fearful outrage as those now enacting at Amoy and its neighbourhood. The imperialists have retaken the place, and have marked their success by slaying in cold blood

nearly 1 ,000 persons, most of whom took no part in the late movement except on compulsion. The streets and wharves of Ainoy have literally streamed with human blood, not shed in any warlike operations, but done in savage revenge and to blind the authorities at Pekin as to the bravery of the enactors. A letter froin Amoy, dated Nov. 22, received but a few hours ago, states that up to that period all was quiet, and matters wore much the same appearance, as far as foreigners were concerned, as under the insurgent rulers. Executions were of daily occurrence. The Mandarins, to mark their success, were revelling in human gore, putting to death all who fall into their hands indiscriminately. The original mover of the rebellion had been given up to the Mandarins ; the unfortunate wretch was executed on the 17th November, together with his son, both bodies being quartered and their heads placed on the principal city gates. The villages around Amoy were made to contribute to the monster executions. Whole villages were threatened with death, unless they gave up all who took part in or sympathised with the rebels, and as a consequence of this brutal demand the poor, weak, inoffensive, and defenceless villages were surrendered up as victims to satiate the mandarins' thirst for blood. From these heart-rending and revolting scenes one gladly turns to notice the progress which the great movement is making in the interior. We have very little certain information of the doings of the Nanking insurgents ; but one thing is clear,

namely, that their cause is making headway, notwithstanding all the resources of the emperor are directed to quell the wide spread of disaffection. It is generally believed that the emperor is besieged in Pekin, and various rumours are current that the Tartar ruler has actually fled his capital, but of this no certain information has been received. On the subject of the present position and prospects of the groat movement, the Friend of China is of opinion that the Tartar dynasty is now at its last gasp ; and that the next Chinese year will not unwarrantable be called as the reign of Hungtseu-tsieuen, the Prince of Peace.

From the St. Thomas Times, Feb. 15, 1854. Disnppcaraitce of tlic Cholera. The very satisfactory account we were enabled to give in our last issue regarding the disappearance of Cholera here, we ate happy to say warrants confirmation this day. We have had seven deaths since Saturday noon þÿ I wo of them from Fever, two of Consumption, and three pronounced as cases of Cholera ; but every one in this community must he aware that alarmed and panic-ridden with ideas of Cholera as we are. and have been, it is no very difficult matter for the imagination to fancy ever v death now occurring in the Island to be occasioned by Choleta, and ibis feeling is certain to live in the minds of men for some time to come, ft resembles the sensations we endure after a severe Earthquake, for every carriage or waggon that rolls along the stieets after that alaims us, and causes us to think that another Earthquake is occurring, and such feelings will exist until time weais them off i he mind The same is the case after a hurricane, every gust of wind that succeeds it makes the system nervous, and so it will he with the imagination in regard to Cholera ; every death that passes our doors for the future will bring to our memories the horrid spectacles of Cholera we have witnessed, and nothing will eradicate these distressing recollections but lime. And, therefore, is it high time, we think, that the Health Officer, and the different Consuls accredited here, begin to grant Clean Bills of Health, for " as one Swallow does not make a
summer," neither does a solitary case of Cholera, after a fortnight's gradual disappearance of the disease, endanger the bonne sante of a community.

From the Weekly Record, Grenada, Feb. 9. INTER-COLONIAL. W E regret to learn from our papers, and from private accounts, that there had been some unfortunate occurrences in a few of the neighbouring Islands, since the removal of the troops. In St. Vincent, the " Strike" which we gave the particulars of last week, we regret to state still continued, and in one or two instances, the laborers had proceeded to acts of violence in destroying some carts with their contents, and intimidating by threats, others of the laborers who had not joined in the Strike for higher-wages. In Tobago, we learn from the following extract from a letter received at St. Vincent, dated at Scarborough, 24th January, that attempts had been made to set the Town on Fire : þÿ

the 16th. They have appointed a general Police force but to no effect. On Saturday night, the 21st, the Barbadians that are at present in the island joined together to set the Town on fire that night, but luckily one of them, who by appearance seems to be pretty respectable, came in that day and reported to the officers of Police. They directly apprehended the head person who was the instigator of the matter, and in examining his house they found a quantity of Gun Powder and Shavings. He is now in Gaol for Sessions, and they are threatening to take our lives þÿ that is þÿ the colored and white men." And, by private accounts from Dominica, wc regret to learn that some serious riots had occurred there, and that the return of the Troops recently removed had been prayed for. There are doubtless, in every community, some diabolical characters who may attempt to work on the minds of the lower orders, and induce them to commit acts of violence ; we, however, trust that Grenada, may be an exception. Unanimity prevails amongst all classes, and we have every confidence in the good sense and feeling of our peasantry to assert that there need be no apprehension of their resorting to any of those acts which are recorded as having taken place elsewhere. We regret to learn that Yellow Fever had again broken out at Antigua, and that several deaths had taken place, particularly in the Garrison ; Captain Marston of the Royal Artillery and his wife, are among the victims. -TlOiS- From the Palladium, Jan. 14.

The inhabitants of Martinique seem to take a peculiar pride in their little fleet of inter-colonial steamers, and an event of some importance has just occured to enhance the advantages which may be derived from their presence in these seas. It appears that the new Steamer Madadina had left St. Pierre in the beginning of December, on a trip among the Islands, and had reached St. Thomas on the 8th of that month. The next day the authorities of that Island received intelligence that a large ship was making signals of distress, to the North West, and a determination was immediately come to by the French Consul and Captain Bocande, Commander of the Madadina, that the latter should proceed to the assistance of the vessel. This lie did with praiseworthy promptitude, taking with him some English and American gentlemen who were anxious to learn to what nation she helonged. In a couple of hours the Madadina came within hail of the ship in distress, which proved to be the American Packet, Atlas, of 1000 tons burden, bound from Havre to New Orleans, and having on board 350 emigrants, and a rich cargo of French merchandize. She had been 48 days at sea, and about fifteen days

® stirz A t i before, had encountered a severe gale of wind, whereby she got dismasted and otherwise sustained much damage. The loss of her rigging and sails was but scantily supplied; she remained during three days in imminent danger; and owing to an insufficiency of food and the filthy state of the emigrants, 38 of them had died. At last the Trade Winds had driven her within fifteen miles of St. Thomas, and there seemed little doubt that she would have become a total wreck, tint for the opportune assistance of the Madadina. Captain Bocande immediately set to work, and by great exertions, succeeded in towing the Atlas into St. Thomas, where they came to anchor at half-past 7, p. M., on the same day. There is an incident connected with this affair, which should not be passed " The Troops have been removed from here on over in silence. It seems that the Captain of the4/to, in the true spirit of his nation, would not allow the Captain of the Madadina to take the wreck in tow, until he was first informed of the amount of salvage he should have to pay ; and that Captain Bocande, with sentiments alike creditable to his nation and himself, refused to make any bargain until the claims of humanity had received his first attention þÿ proposing at the same time to leave the question to the decision of the French and American Consuls at St. Thomas. But the American Captain would not consent to have either his ship or his passengers saved, unless the price were determined beforehand. He then made an offer to Captain Bocande of

five hundred dollars, but the latter indignantly refused to listen to any stipulation. At last, Mr. Ridgway, an American merchant, who was on board of the Madadina, succeeded, at great personal risk, in ascending the wreck, anil with much difficulty prevailed upon his compatriot to postpone the question of dollars, and attend to the safety of saving of passengers and sinking ship ! We extract these particulars from the published Report of Captain Bocande, in the hope that they may receive from our contemporaries the publicity which they deserve. The only punishment that the friends of public decency can inflict on those American Sea-Captains and the spirit of dollarism to which the rights of humanity are daily sacrificed by men of that class, is to publish the disgusting facts to the world at large. We forgot to mention that the first intelligence of the affair of the Atlas was communicated to the inhabitants of Martinique by our fellow towns-man, that active and enterprising Navigator þÿ Captain Glaudon of the Qtteely Shiel.

ST. JOHNS. Cholera, of which I spoke on 20th instant, seems determined to baffle all human efforts in our island to resist its attacks on the labouring classes. It follows, of course, that all work relating to sugar cultivation has suddenly ceased ; and so far has the mysterious pestilence disorganised our sugar estates, are that with some properties pasture-men on difficulty found to keep the cattle from feeding upon that which, to our unprosperous planters, is stock and store. The Estates Adrian and Hermann Farm, that, from the elevated site they occupy, enjoy a mild and delightful climate, and have been, hitherto, considered healthy, present to-day a scene of intense suffering and desolation, in despite of every exertion of our watchful and beloved Judge repel to the fearful visitant. For the St. Croix Avis. Some men's situation in life often screens them from that rebuke and contempt due to

their immoral and impolite behaviour, which, however, when manifested by individuals of another class, always meet with its desert ; even from those very persons who are directly guilty of the same practices. Politeness and affability of manners are, in our conception, the natural results of an enlightened and timely education ; and are some of the fruits by which we may rightly judge of the mental and intellectual qualities of pretensions to gentility. It is, however, in this very position, where men are most anxious to maintain a patrician spirit, that we invariably witness and encounter such acts of impoliteness and immorality as would disgrace the character of the barbarous ; yea. of the savage. It is not, we say, a feasible matter in such cases to correct these evils by awarding the perpetrators thereof the rebuke and correction which they deservedly merit; hence pride, arrogance, self-aggrandizement, and even despotism, often usurp the place of that courteous and unassuming gentility, which we reasonably expect in the upper ranks of life. People in general, while thev rightly disapprove of such unbecoming conduct in the lower order of society, often find some approving terms by which they nominate, and even applaud, the same conduct in tire opposite rank; covering thereby many things which deserve censure and exposuie Is one of the " tiptops a bad pay-master " what do people say of him? þÿ " He is too busy to attend to such trifles." is he manifesting hauteur and arrogance in his manners, what

then7 þÿ A man in his sphere of life must maintain a certain dignity." Does he scorn and avoid the approaches of the poor, what Ihen ? þÿ " He did not notice," or " he is near sighted;" particularly if he happen to wear the mark of his suddenly shammed organic defect, (spectacles ) Does he omit to return the polite salutation proffered him even to a degree ofmenial subserviency ? þÿ " He was in thought at the moment." Is he peevish, despotic, and overbearing towards his inferiors? þÿ " He is a little eccentric, but in general a very good man." Does he dispense his wealth to compensate for the satiating of his wicked and immoral desires, thereby apparently set ving others, while he has his own ends in view I þÿ " He is an exceedingly charitable man." When they would invite him to attend some particular religious festival, which Ins sta- do tion compels him to countenance, what people say þÿ? In tact, another co- " lour is given to all his actionR, however gross, base, or inconsistent. We cannot, however, boast of any attainment in this deceptive art of misrepresenting the faulty and censurable behaviour of such individuals; for we have learnt in the school of common sense and everv-day experience to view the defective traits of these nabobs" " in their true light; and while wo will duly lence in their possessors, we will ever feel appreciate real moral worth and true excel- it
imperative on us to shun, despise, contemn and censure þÿ although wc dare not openly rebuke þÿ such admixtures of vulgarism and gentility. A Lookeu-on.

From the Observer, January I, 1854. TIIE DISASTER AT SINOPE. The reports brought by the English and French Bteamers from Sinope had caused the greatest ! consternation in Constantinople. Nothing is left of the Turkish ships but heaps of fragments. Of j the crews, which amounted to 5,000 men, at most only 1,500 are alive. From the 23rd of Nov. three Russian ships of the line cruised during four days in sight of Sinope On the 29th a reinforcement of three three-deckers, two other ships of the line, two frigates, and four steamers arrived, and on the following day, at noon, the Russian flag-ship summoned the Turks to surrender. For some time the Russians were completely sheltered from the guns of the strand batteries by the Turkish ships, "and, as the liners fired from a distance, they suffered very little from the lighter metal of the frigates." The Turks, having at last cut their cables, and let their ships drift on shore, the strand batteries opened their fire. The Russians then began to shell the town, which, with the frigates, was soon in flames. " This was a fearful moment. The sea of fire, the roaring of the artillery, the continual explosions, and the fragments of human bodies which were hurled about in all directions in the air, formed one of the most fearful spectacles man ever beheld." The Turkish quarter was completely burnt, and the houses in the other part of the town, where no bombs had fallen, were perforated with balls. The corpse of Hussein Ramsi Pasha, the Turkish Rear-Admiral, was found in the water the next

morning. All the employes left the town ecxepting M.-Pirjanz, the Austrian Consul, to whom the Russian Kornileff wrote, principally attributing the misfortune which had befallen the town to the explosion of the ships, " which he said the Turks themselves had set on fire." It was added that the Russians had no intention to take possession of the place, their only object being to put it out of the power of the Turkish fleet again and " commit piracy." The Russian fleet had to convey ammunition to the coast of Circassia, left Sinope before the French and English vessels arrived, but eye-witnesses stated that it had not suffered much, as it lay almost out of range of the guns of the frigates. A British trader which lay in the port had two men killed by shots from the Russian ships, and, being subsequently run foul of by a burning 1 urkish frigate, she was destroyed. Her captain and crew, who escaped, say that the Turks "fought like devils," blowing up their own ships rather than that they should fall into the
3 tr It O 2 31 A T '1 3 hands of the Russians. The ships of the line poured in such tremendous broadsides that the decks of the Turkish vessels were literally carried overboard.

BATTLE SCENES. The following is an account given by Major Bevan, in his work Thirty Years in India , of a scene which occurred at the conclusion of a battle in which he was engaged : þÿ " Near midnight, when about to retire to rest, an order was received from the coramander-in chief, to detach an officer and 100 pioneers for the purpose of collecting the wounded, and also such arms and accoutrements as could be found on the field of battle. This severe duty devolved upon me, as the other officers were all laid up from the fatigue they had undergone throughout the day. Several palanquins belonging to the head-quarters and stall were kindly sent to bring in the wounded, as none of the public dooly-boys could be procured, they having dispersed in search of plunder. 1 The scenes of wo and misery I experienced during this dark and dismal night, in my progress over the field of battle admist the carnage of the day, will never be effaced from my memory. ' The groans and screams of the wounded and dying constantly struck my ear, as also the piteous wailings of the wives, daughters, fathers, or sons, of those who had fallen, or the cries of others in search of their missing relatives. With these heart-rending sounds were often mixed the wild execrations of the dying, who were attempting to repel the marauders who came for the purpose of plunder ' W e found rapine. and many bodies of our own soldiers in a perfect state of nudity, which plainly evinced they had not escaped those indignities offered to

the dead and dying by the profligate followers of a camp. ' Our enemies were treated in the same manner ; the wretches who wandered over the field in search of plunder spared neither friend nor foe when there was a prospect of booty. We rescued a considerable number of the wounded from this lonely death, the most terrible to the imagination ; but several of them had fallen victims to the cowardly assassins or the inclemency of the weather before we could afford them rescue or relief. The ground was soft clay, which had been saturated by the heavy rains and trodden into a quagmire by the passing and repassing of men, animals, and carriages ; a misty, drizzling rain fell incessantly, and these circumstances rendered our toil exceedingly difficult and tedious. We had to wait a considerable time for the return of the palanquins from the field-hospital, whither our wounded were conveyed, so that the morning dawned ere our task was completed. ' The scenes which I witnessed in the hospital were less harrowing to the feelings than those in the field. Dr. A and the rest of the medical staff employed all that skill and energy could suggest for the relief of the sufferers. I saw them perform several very difficult operations and amputations, and especially one on Lieutenant H , whose knee was severely shattered. He sustained the operation with unflinching courage, but expired soon after it had been completed. Few, indeed, of thoso who had received gunshot wounds survived, for the fractures they had suf-

fered were generally so extensive as to bring on locked-jaw. Many young aspirants for military fame, dazzled by " the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war," would have their ardour sadly damped by witnessing the scenes on the field and in the hospital of Maheidpoor.' Captain Patterson of the 50th, or Queen's Own Regiment, presents in his Adventures a description of what came under his observation during the war in the Peninsula, which is equally affecting. As the narration of such incidents may be of use in creating a just horror of war, we here offer it for the perusal of the reader : þÿ

' Soon after nightfall, and when the clash o arms was no longer heard, an interment of the dead took place, and many a poor fellow, who had a few hours before been full of life and strength, was now deposited in his narrow bed. The remains of Major Stanhope were lowered to the grave by his brother-officers and comrades with their sashes. He had worn this day a suit of new uniform, and a pair of bright silver epaulets ; in which, with his military cloak around him, upon the same hour as his lamented chief, he was consigned ' While we were engaged in the performance of to an honourable tomb. this melancholy duty, the Honourable Captain Stanhope, of the Guards, aid-de-camp to Sir John Moore, rode up, directed by the torch-light, to the mournful group. It was the first intimation which he received of his brave relation's fate Dismounting, and overcome with grief, he took a last farewell ; and having obtained his ring, together with a lock of hair, he tore himself hastily away from the heart-rending scene. ' On our march across this ground, an incident occurred which made a deep impression on the minds of those who happened to be present at the time. Across the pathway, and on either side, men and officers were lying ; and one of the latter was extended on his face among the heath and brushwood, so close to where we passed, that Major Malcolm Mackenzie of the 70th, prompted as it were by intuition, suddenly dismounted to ascertain who was the individual. Stooping to observe the features, that were partly concealed

by the long broom, he started back with grief and consternation, on perceiving that the young soldier, who had thus fallen an early victim, was his brother, Lieutenant Colin Mackenzie, of the same regiment. ' A party of the officers of the 50th, who were collected in a knot discussing the affairs of the eventful day, were quickly seen by those marksmen, who, from behind the rocks, despatched with deadly aim a few rifle missiles, each with its billet ; and the balls were so faithful to their errand, that the congress was soon of the members being sent to " that bourne from dissolved, some which no traveller returns," and the remainder wounded. Among those who fell on this occasion, was Lieutenant Hugh Birshall, of the fourth battalion company, which he had commanded for some time. Having fallen ill, he was in his bed at Elizondo when the battle commenced ; and hearing the noise of musketry, he thought that something was going forward in the lines in which ho ought to bear a part. With a mind indued with a strength superior to that of his weakly frame, he arose from the couch of sickness, and calling all the vigour that he could muster to his aid, tottered with feeble pace to the field of action, arriving at a late hour upon the hill. Exhausted, pale, and like one risen from the dead, he resumed his former place ; and scarcely had he joined the group assembled in the front, when, by a fatal bullet, this spirited young man was numbered with the slain.' þÿ Chambers'' s Pocket Miscellany

- » GEORGE III. AND MR DAY. When Judge Day returned from India, the prime minister represented to his majesty that knighthood was an honour to which the judge was entitled. ' Poh, poh.' said his majesty, 1 cannot turn day into night ; it is impossible.' At the next levee, which was about Christmas, his majesty was again entreated to knight Mr. Day. The king inquired if he was married, and was answered in the affirmative. Well, well,' said the monarch 'then let him be introduced, and I will work a couple of miracles ; I will not only turn Day into Knight, but 1 will also make Lady Day at Christmas.'

Perilous Encounter with a Shark. þÿ On the 29th of April, while five young soldiers, stationed at Corfu, were sailing along at a rapid rate, the boat in which they were, received a sudden shock, as if it had run upon a rock, which nearly capsized her. One of the soldiers having looked over the side, perceived a large shark swimming close to the boat, but it disappeared on his throwing a bottle at it. A number of porpoises were also about, and one of these was harpooned by a soldier named Flowers, son of Mr. Flowers, chimney-sweeper, Theatre-street, Warwick. On being struck the porpoise immediately dived, and the line being entangled round the arm of a soldier named Hanson, lie was dragged into the water. Flowers seeing Hanson about thirty yards from the boat making for a rock, turned the boat in that direction and nearly overtook him -r but, when within about six yards of him one of his companions cried out that there was a shaik going towards Hanson, Flowers seized a knife which stuck in the side of t he boat, plunged head first into ihe water, and diving under-neath the shark, turned himself on his hack, and thrust the knife into the belly of the monster in several places ; but it was of little use, the shark having siezed upon Hanson, and taken his leg ofl near the knee. Flowers then endeavoured lo get his comrade on his back, but both of them were nearly exhausted. He succeeded, however, in getting him into the boat, and bound up the wound with Ins shirt. When they reached the hospital their

unfortunate comrade was nearly dead from exhaustion, but after a short time recovered. When on their way they captured the wounded shark, and towed it on shore. It weighed 234 lbs., and when opened the leg was found in its throat, the bone mangled to bits. The body of tire shark has been placed in i he Sailors' Home at Corfu.

Derivation of News þÿ It is just two years since t he word News was stated lo be derived from the initial letters of the cardinal points of the compass, as prefixed to early newspapers. 1 well remember the impression which the statement made on me, if written seriously, as a mark of credulity ; if sportively, as rattier out of place Moreover, it was Loth slated as a fact, and as an ingenious þÿetymology a manifest inconsistency. In the fierce and tiresome discussion which arose out of that announcement, the main points in support of the asserted derivation were never once introduced. Do such caily newspapers exist ? Is the derivation itself of eailv date? As to the first question, 1 must declare that no such newspapers ever came under my observation ; hut as lo the second, it must be admitted that the derivation has been in print, with all the weight of evidence which belongs to it, above two centuries. 1 shall assume, if not belter informed, that it has no other authority than the subjoined epigram in Wits Recreations, first published in 1640, and said to contain the finest fancies of the muses of those limes. In default of the original edition of that rare work, I transcribe ftom the republication of it in 1817. " News When news doth come, if any would discuss | The letter of the word, resolve it thus : News is couvey'd by letter, word, or mouth, " And comes to us from North, East, West, and South

To tlic Planters ot St. Croix. If the Cholera should come among you, the author of these lines thinks that the following remarks, based upon two week's dearly bought experience, may prove useful, and the means of saving many lives among your labourers.

Any estate having a sickhouse, as yet in such a state, as to receive a reasonable proportion of your gang, should have it put immediately in order; have a place made where fire can be kept up, to boil and warm any thing required. Have a parcel of blankets ready ; as such a thing now a-davs is scarce among the negroes. If no sickhouse remains, any other building may do, the boilinghouse for instance, as you may be sure, as long as the Cholera is on the estate you will have no other use for it. Of course you will have all the requisite medicines &o., at hand. The authorities here, who since the commencement of the disease have, in every respect, shown an activity and energy, which perhaps no other place unprepared for such an evil can boast of, published under the 19th December a direction as to what was to be done where medical assistance could not be had. 'This has been the case here, and will be the case with you also, as it is impossible for any medical man to attend but to a few cases on the estate, particularly those fur from town. Fix upon half a dozen trusty hands, who from being promised very liberal remuneration will aet as sick nurses, and if you could persuade them that the Cholera is not contagious, which conviction 1 myself havp, it would be so much the better, to which purpose, nothing is more efficient than for oneself to be among the sick. 1 suppose that at the fiist 2 or 3 deaihs you will have the greatest trouble, and perhaps be obliged to make use of force, to pre-

vent the family from having the corpse washed, dressed, as customary. Be firm in opposing this. The moment the patient censes to breathe let him be put in the coffin, which may be left uncovered for some hours þÿ If there is any danger of this disease being contagious. 1 think it is propagated, by washing or handling the dead. þÿ This mvsteiy I leave to the more learned to solve, myself not having any knowledge of the matter, but only give this as my opinion. As it is nearly impossible to prevent the neerocs from using their own remedies, which consist in many sorts of green herbs and especially green guavas the utmost surveillance is necessary. They place much more confidence in their own prescriptions than in those of the physician. By following this I think you can not well do more, only warn your people to come immediately at the very first symptoms of vomiiing, sick stomach or diarthae. I will name the rases, which 1 have had during the Inst fortnight. The estate is so far from town, that the distance prevents any medical man from attending it. 1. A boy 13 years old, the first taken sick here, on the 7th inst. He died the day after. It was ascertained that the same boy, the day before taken ill, had eaten papaws abundantly, and was seen vomiting in the afternoon, but 1 was not acquainted with his illness until next morning. 2 A girl of 5 years, taken very ill the 9ih, was well 3 days after. 3. A woman about 45, taken ill the 10th, was well the 13th. 4. A young man of about 23, the worst case
I have seen as to vomiting, diarrhae and cramps, was taken sick the 13th. He is, out now. 5 A young man about the same age, taken

sick the same day, but with less severe symptoms is out now. 6. Another young man, same age, taken very severely ill on the same day, is well now 7. A woman about 26, delivered 3| months ago taken sick on the 15th. þÿ She died the day after. Long before her accouchement she had never been out of her house, being very indolent I was called to her at 12 in the night, and found her extremely ill, with the child at her breast sucking. Taking her in hand 1 removed the baby to another room, giving it to an old woman, to take care of, but an hour after another woman having a young child, unknown to me, took this very child and nursed it, which she has done ever since and both being well, I think is a striking proof of t he Cholera not being contagious, as the child had certainly been more than 8 hours at the the mother's side, when she was severely attacked. 8 A strong man of 34. the driver on the estate taken ill on the 8th. lie was very severely attacked, but was up on the 12th, out the 16th and 1 considered him entirely well. His wife (No. 9) got sick on the 17th and this man, took his horse on the 18th, arid against my remonstrances and advice went to town to buy funeral clothes for his wife He fell from the horse near town, was taken up and brought to the hospital, where 1 am told lie died 12 houts after. 9 A woman about 30, Was taken sick the 17th, the 18th in the morning she was very low. At 4 r jr., I found her a little better, having begun to perspire, and 1 then iiad hopes of her recovery,

having several friends about her, she had plenty of rubbing and attendance. She expired a couple of hours after 1 had seen her. and 1 then heard that her frier ds who well knew, that no washing would be allowed after death, hud washed her short ly after I left her, to which 1 attribute her death. 10. An old man of 60 or more, very strong and active. 1 met him on the 17th at daybreak, coming God knows from where, wet from the rain He told me that lie felt sick. 1 ordered him to bed immediately but be would lake no medicine, would not allow any body to touch him. He expired in the afternoon. 11 An old woman about 05 Taken siek same da \ , died in the afternoon. Neither she would toko anything, hut spit out anything that was forced in her mouth. She also died the same afternoon. 12 A strong man 36, taken sick the 20ih about noon, died in the evening. 13. An old woman 65, taken sick the 20th, died next day. 14 A young woman 24, taken sick the same day and died in the evening. Besides these 14 severe cases, I have had 10 or 12 more or less attacked, of which 3 at this moment 1 have no great hopes, I am fully convinced, that several of these people had been sick at least some hours before I was acquainted of it ; but 1 must leave it to the medical men, to decide, whether a few hours enn make any difference, which 1 believe they do. St. Thomas the 22nd January 1854. A SI. Thomas Planter

WORK FIRST, AND FAST AFTERWARDS. Lord Palmcrston has been unfortunate enough to incur the fierce displeasure of the Established Presbytery of Edinburgh, because he will not indulge their Reverences with the appointment of a National Fast, on account of the visitation of the cholera ; but, instead thereof, takes occasion to direct a very sensible and statesmanlike letter to the Moderator of that Reverend body, pointing out the duty incumbent on all classes to take those practical means which Providence has placed within the reach of all for averting the spread of the devastating scourge. The following is a copy of the correspondence on the subject, which was read at the meeting of Presbytery on Wednesday last: ' Edinburgh, Oct. 15th, 1853. þÿ My Lord, þÿ At a meeting of the ltov. the Presbytery of Edinburgh, on the 13th curt, there was some discussion as to the propriety of appointing, on ecclesiastical authority, a day for prayer and humiliation within the bounds of the Presbytery, under the visitation of Asiatic Cholera, which has again ap-

peared in this country. The members were of opinion that it was likely in the circumstances, that a national last would be appointed by Royal authority. For this reason they delayed making an appointment for this locality, and directed me, in the meantime, respectfully to request that you would be pleased to say þÿ if you feel yourself at liberty to do so þÿ whether the appointment of a national fast by the Queen is in contemplation. The Presbytery hoped to be excused for the liberty they use in preferring this request. þÿ I have the honour to be, my Lord, your Lordship's humble servant, W. II. Gray, Moderator of the Presbytery of Edinburgh. þÿ To the Right Hon. Viscount Palmerstou, M. P., tj-c.' ' Whitehall, Oct. 19, 1853. þÿ'Sir I am directed by Viscount Palmerston to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 15th instant, requesting, on behalf of the Presbytery of Edinburgh, to be informed whether it is proposed to appoint a day ol' national fast on account of the visitation of the cholera, and to state that there can he no doubt that manifestations of humble resignation to the Divine Will, and sincere acknowledgements of human unworthiness are never more appropriate than when it has pleased Providence to afflict mankind with some severe visitation ; but it does not appear to Lord Palmcrston that a national fast would be suitable to the circumstances of the present moment. The Maker of the Universe has established certain laws of nature for the planet in which we live,

and the weal or woe of mankind depends upon the observance or the neglect of those laws. One of those laws connects health with the absence of those gasseous exhalations which proceed from overcrowded human beings ; from decomposing substances, whether animal or vegetable, and those same laws render sickness the almost inevitable consequence of exposure to those noxious influences. But it has at the same time pleased Providence to place it within the power of man to make such arrangements as will prevent ordisperse such exhalations so as to render them harmless, aud it is the duty of man to attend to those laws of nature, and to exert the faculties which Providence has thus given to man for his own welfare. The recent visitation of cholera, which has for the moment been mercifully checked, is an awful warning given to the people of this realm that they have too much neglected their duty in this respect, and that those persons with whom it rested to purify towns and cities, and to prevent or to remove the causes of disease, have not been sufficiently active in regard to such matters. Lord Palmerston would, therefore, suggest that the best course which the people of this country can pursue to deserve that the further progress of the cholera should be stayed, will be to employ the interval that will elapse between the present time and the beginning of next spring in planning and executing measures by which those portions of their towns and cities which are inhabited by the poorest classes, and which, from the nature

of things, must most need purification and improvement may he freed from those causes and sources of contagion which, if allowed to remain, will infallibly breed pestilence, and be fruitful in death, in spite of all the prayers and fastings of an united but inactive nation. When man has done his utmost for his own safety, then is the time to invoke the blessing of Heaven to give effect to his exertions. þÿ I am, Sir, your obedient servant, Henry Fitzroy. þÿ To the Rev. W. H Gray, Moderator of the Edinburgh Presbytery.'

New York Times. GREAT FIRE AT NEW YORK. On the 10th Dec. the most extensive confla- j gration that has happened in New York since the great fire of 1846, broke out in the premises of Messrs. Harper and Brothers, the celebrated American publishers. The accident was occasioned by a plumber,) who was at work in one of the lower storeys, and who, after lighting his pipe, threw the burning paper into a vessel of camphine which he had mistaken for water. Instantly the place was in flames. Fed with combustible materials on every side, they soon raged with volcanic fury. There was scarcely time for the occupants of the vast building to escape with their lives. Fortunately, out of the 650 employes within its walls, some 400 had not returned from dinner, those who remained being chiefly the young women employed in the press-rooms and bindery. Thanks to the daring efforts of the firemen, whose first efforts were directed to saving life, these were all rescued from a dreadful fate, though one of the number was so much injured that she died on the way to the hospital. Several other persons were more or less injured. No fewer than 2,000 men, women, and children, have been thrown out of employment by this catastrophe. The ravages of the fire were not confined to Messrs. Harper's establishment, but extended to the neighbouring premises. The Walton Hotel, an extensive edifice, built a hundred years ago by a gentleman of that name, but which has of late been an emigrants' boarding-house, was also com-

pletely destroyed. The following is the estimate of the property of the Harpers, lost and saved : þÿ Property in the buildings: þÿ The bindery establishment, estimated to be worth about $60,000 ; 35 Adams presses, valued at $75,000 ; 9 hydraulic presses, $15,000; materials in the composing-room, $15,000 ; the stereotype foundry and electrotype apparatus, $5,000 ; printed sheets of the Pictorial Bibles, half of which was owned by J. G. Adams, $30,000 ; steam-engine and boiler, $5,000 ; stock of books and printed sheets, estimated in the inventory to be worth not far from $800,000 ; woodcuts, estimated at $50,000 ; ten buildings, worth probably $150,000 ; stereotype plates, valued at $400,000 ; total property, $ 1 ,655,000. Property saved : þÿ Stereotype plates, $400,000 ; woodcuts (probably), $40,000 ; books, paper, and miscellaneous, $10,000; total saved, þÿ$450,000 total loss, $1,205,000. On this amount the insurance does not exceed $250,000. The establisment of the Harpers was founded by James Harper, the eldest of four brothers, who now constitute the firm. He came to the city in 1810, a lad 15 years old, and served an apprenticeship of six years to Paul and Thomas, the leading printers of the day. His brother John soon followed him, and learned the trade of Mr. Seymour, a printer, in John-street. In 1817, with the small capital James had saved, the brothers opened a small book and job-office in Dover-street. The first book they printed was " Seneca's Morals," the second was an edition of

the Methodist Catechism. The first book they published on their account was Locke's F.ssay " on the Human Understanding." They toiled with unremitting industry, and maintained the highest character for enterprise and integrity. In 1820, the third brother, Joseph Wesley, joined them, and six years later Fletcher became a member of the firm. From that time until now they have carried on the publishing business with a degree of well-directed energy which has few parallels. They removed to Cliff-street about 1820, and have added one building after another to their establishment as the demands of their business required. The amount of books they have issued is almost incalculable. For the last few years they have published, on an average, twenty-five volumes a minute for ten hours a day ;

Harpers' premises the fire extended to many others in Cliff street, and the consequence was the destruction of property to the extent of $1,500,000, and the burning of fifteen houses

The Sin and lolly of Scolding. 1. It is evil, and only evil, and lhat continually. David understood human nature and says, " Fret not thyself in any wise to do evil." That is, if you cannot speak without scolding, keep silence. 2 It Destroys Affection. þÿ No one ever did endure or ever will love an habitual fretter, fault-finder, or scolder. Husbands, wives, children, relatives, or domestics have no affection for the peevish, fretful, faultfinders. Few tears are shed over the graves of such. Persons of high moral principle may tolerate them þÿ may bear with them But they cannot love them more than the sting of nettles, or the noise of mosquitoes. Many a man lias been driven to the taverr and to dissipatiou, by a peevish fretlul wife. Many a wife has been made miserable by a peevish fretful husband. 3. It is the Bane of Domestic Happiness. þÿ A fretful, peevish, complaining, faultfinding person in a family, is like the continual chafing in an inflamed sore. Wo to the man, woman or child, who is exposed to the influence of such a temper in another. Five tenths of all domestic trials and uuhappincss spring from this source. Mrs. D. is of this temperament. She wonders Iter husband is not more fond of her company. That her children give her so much trouble. That domestics do not like to work for her. That she cannot secure the good will of young people. The truth is, she is fretful and peevish, Children fear her, and do not love her. She never yet gained the affections of a young person, nor ever will till she leaves off helling

4. It Defeats the End of Family Government. þÿ Good family government is the blending authority will) affection, so as to secure respect and love ; indeed, this is the great secret of managing young people Now your fretters may inspire fear, but they always make two faults where they correct one. Scolding at a child, Letting at a child, sneering at a child, tnunting a child, as though it had no fechogs, inspires dread and dislike, and fosters those very dispositions from which many of the faults of childhood pioceed. þÿ Mr. G. and Mis. F. are of this class. Their children nre made to mind ; but how ? Mrs. F. frets and scolds her children. Site is severe enough upon their faults. She seems to watch them in order to find fault. She sneers at them þÿ treats them as though they had no feelings. She seldom gives them a command without a threat, and a long running, fault-finding commentary. When she chides, it is not done in a dignified manner. She raises her voice, puts on a cross look, threatens, strikes them, pinches their ears, slaps their hands, &c. The children cry, pout, sulk, and poor Mrs F. has to do her work over pretty often. Then she will find fault with her husband, because he docs not fall in with her ways, or chime with her as a chorus. 5. Fretting and Scolding makes Hypocrites. þÿ As a fretter never receives confidence and affection, so no one likes to tell

them anything disagreeable, and thus procure for themselves a fretting. þÿ Now children conceal, in as much as they cannot make up their minds to be frank and open-hearted. So husbands conceal from their wives, and wives from their husbands. For a man may brave a lion, but he likes not to come in contact with nettles and musquitoes. g. It Destroys one's Peace of Mind. þÿ The more one frets, the more he may. A fretter will always have enough to fret at. Especially if he or she has the bump of order and neatness largely developed, something will always be out of place. There will always be some dirt somewhere. Others will not eat right, look right, talk þÿright he will not do those things so as to please them. And fretters nre generally so selfish as to have no tegard for any one's comfort but their own. 7. It is a Mark of a Vulgar Disposition. þÿ Some persons have so much gall in their disposition, are so selfish, lhat they have no regard to the feelings of others. All things must be done to please them. They make their husbands, wives, children, domestics, the conductors by which their spleen and illnature is discharged. Woe to the children who are exposed to such þÿinfluences it makes them callous and unfeeling, and when they grow up, they pursue the same course with their children, or those entrusted to their management ; and thus the race of freltcrs is perpetuated.

When Cholera is abroad, accomplishing its deadly purpose, and every report that comes to us is a register of death, silence may be considered an indication of, if Dot a total disappearance of the evil, at least a change for the better þÿ hence my silence daring the past week. Fortunately, I resume my pen under favorable circumstances, for the reports that now reach mo from the quarters where the disease still exists, shew a decided improvement in the public health, and a manifest decline in tho effects of a pestilence that oarrics devastation to the remotest oorners.

Let us now devoutly hope that the Divine command, þÿ so far shalt thou go, and no further þÿ! has gone forth to stay the progress of the evil, and that soon our care-worn Planters will be enabled to compose the minds of their remaining laborers, and to restore order on their estates, which have been so violently shaken by the calamity. Through the provident care of our affectionate sister, þÿ St. þÿThomas, wc have come in possession of a fine stock of Medicines, consisting of Chalk Mixtures, Camphor, Laudanum, Castor-oil, Brandy, and, þÿtho last, not least, of Dr. þÿSecchi s ELIXIR ! þÿ for which we shall never re-pay you. þÿ Alas ! the grateful heart never pays þÿ it always þÿowes. There is no task more pleasing in the sight of God, or more delightful to the soul of man, than the one of attempting to mould the public mind þÿ to lighten its path in a correct course þÿ and to endeavour, with a sincerity of purpose, to re-kindle into a flame the embers of good , which, happily, only slumber in the breast of mankind. The attempt, however laudable at all times, is infinitely so in the presence of circumstances which render it inexpedient to employ the use of argument to arouse the dormant sensibilities of human nature. On looking around, the scenes of desolation and misery which present themselves every where, cannot fail to excite in every breast the most painful emotion and pity ! The instincts of nature are not morbid. The destructive career of the disease has been watched with one common feeling of anxiety and alarm ; and the community bitterly lament the havoc caused by a calamity so overwhelming that many years must elapse before the furrows are closed þÿ the recollection never! þÿ consequently, the feelings of sympathy which exist are in accordance with the Holy precepts. Acts of benevolence arc the true standard of human excellence and nobility þÿ the conviction of a life distinguished by good deeds þÿ Charity to the poor relieves the anguish of the dying bed, and enables the soul to enter the regions of Eternity, fearless, and prepared to meet its Maker ! Whilst we mourned the course of the fearful malady, looking with awe on the gloomy pall

thrown daily on our Island, we trembled ! not for ourselves, but for the preservation of those far dearer to us ! The tidings which at every moment announced the death of some of the victims þÿ the agony of the surviving relatives and friends, creating a shudder in the stoutest hearts ; a fact pourtrayed in the oft repeated and heart-felt expressions, þÿ OGod, spare the þÿunfortunates, and þÿ also our þÿfamilies ! ! ! Spare We live to express the grateful sense of our preservation, and moreover the preservation of those whom we cherish þÿ to express sorrow for the numbers who are at this moment quietly reposing in their narrow and last earthly bed, secure, because beyond the reach of the cares and tempests of stormy life. Pcaeo to their ashes ! Reader ! say, What are the sentiments which these reflections produce on thy mind ? Pardon my presumption when I answer, those which þÿ þÿ/feel in ! the lineament of thy countenance 1 see the throbs of a heart þÿ a soul open to tho sufferings of our fellow men ; if a Man, these emotions will he confined to the cloud which overshadows thy countenance ; if a Woman, the fairest of þÿnature creation, s It will bo marked by the radiant tear ! þÿ Tis charity that bids them come ; The one drops þÿo er tho untimely bier, The other lights the Orphans' home

But however grateful the balm of sympathy to the wounded mind, to those who languish under the weight of great affliction, words are inadequate to convey the relief demanded by the urgency of the ease. We again refer to the article þÿ C'liarily to þÿOrphans., dated the 1st January, published in a former number of this paper. The sum subscribed for that benevolent purpose is far below the object contemplated, from the fact, that since the publication the number of victims is two-fold of what was represented at that period ; hence the necessity of further humane exertions, which cannot prove abortive in a community hitherto foremost to testify a noble sympathy for the Inhabitants of other lands ! When other communities have been visited by calamities such as Earthquakes, Fires, Revolutions, or Diseases, the generous feelings of the mercantile community and others here, have been displayed in a manner which wrung the tears of gratitude from the recipients, while they uttered innumerable blessings on their benefactors. To-day it is our melancholy duty to represent the unfortunate position of our own people ; prostrate on our threshold ; stricken by a visitation as awful as it is unprecedented in the annals of diseases among any nation. Alas ! it is not necessary to dwell on the painful subject you who know þÿ to you who said, with surprise and grief, þÿ I could never suppose that there was so much misery in St. þÿThomas. Therefore, whilst we commend the pledge which has so often been given of the disposition to assist

strangers, we ask to-day that which we believe will be responded to þÿ a similar conduct towards the surviving relatives of those who have perished during the Epidemic þÿ who require assi-tancc þÿ who deserve it þÿ and whose tears of gratitude, and feeling thankfulness, must be as appreciable to of you as those of Strangers ! ! We are aware that a great deal has been done ; individual traits of benevolence and charity have been, and continue to be, shewn amidst our trials. But what are these ? precious it is true, but only dew drops from, Heaven in the great Ocean of trouble and misery ; therefore, the Ministers of every denomination ; every Parent ; every Member of this community, whose circumstances will admit of so doing, will unite in the hallowed task to forward the object of relief to the many Orphans whose Parents have been swept away by the Epidemic. And we conclude with the following impressive remarks : þÿ þÿ The pleasure which affects the human mind with the most lively and transporting touches, is the sense that we act in the eye of infinite wisdom, power, and goodness, that will crown our virtuous endeavours to assist the poor here, with happiness hereafter ; large as our desires, and lasting as our immortal souls, without this the highest state of life is insipid, and with it the lowest is a þÿPARADISE.
