Immigration. þÿ We have so frequently brought l he subject of immigration to our þÿreaders notice, that we fear we may become tiresome in again adverting to it ; and were it not for the important advantages that are involved in the question, we would not encroach on the time and the patience of our friends. It is scarcely necessary for us to refer to the manifold benefits which an extensive stream of immigration would confer upon this Island, but there is one point for consideration which the veriest Tyro cannot fail to concede. If we refer to the past, or the present histories of Nations, it will be lound that the prosperity of a country is entirely dependent upon two þÿthings first, the comparative number of its population with the extent of the land, and, second, the civilization of the people. If we look back to the countries, sav, England and France, we shall there find the population to be so great as to compel a large amount of self-expatriation, as neither tthe soil, nor the other resources of those countries are adequate to the wants of their daily increasing numbers. In England, it is well-known that the amount of the population is so great, that, to use an old saving. þÿ the people tread on each þÿother sheels" meaning, that there is neither employment sufficient for the vast number of hands that require work, or food to support the continuous increase of human life Hence the necessity which drives thousands of her people, annually, from the shores of the British em-

pife irrespective of thut vast tide of immigration which flows into America, California, and Australia, from Continental Europe. When, therefore, we seek to trace the prosperity of a country, the first object that should be sought is, the comparative number of population with the extent of the counliy. To illustrate our argument we shall refer to a given number of acres and a limited number of souls. For example þÿ a run of land containing one thousand acres shall be owned by a man who has a family numbering ten with himself þÿ Assuming that there shall be five persons in that family who are capable, physically, to labour, could that family develop the resources of the thousand acres sufficiently to become prosperous and wealthy, without resorting to the aid of other labour ? assuredly not. But to go yet a little further, and enlarge the sphere of our proposition, we shall suppose that a country is divided into allotments varying from 1600 to 5,000 acres, and, that each allotment becomes vested in but one family, and that each family, only, shall become the cultivators, what then could be the result, in a pecuniary point of view, of such a division? Certain poverty. But why need we draw imaginary, cases, when we have

facts staring us in the face. Here, in Jamaica, we have a most fertile þÿ a prolific country, that yields forth an abundant supply of those things which an all Wise and Bountiful Creator hath provided for man, yet, where is the man who has travelled throughout the country, and who has not witnessed the vast tracks of land that have become ruinates, or the virgin soil protected by its magnificent forest trees þÿ like some proud warrior placed as a guardian þÿo er a þÿ Jilly of the þÿvalley, to shield and screen it from all danger. þÿ But, amidst the desolation of abandoned properties, or even amidst the glorious beauties of þÿnature s virginity, there reigns c silence more fearful than that of death The land is there þÿ decked out in nature's grandest treasures þÿ but whence this solitude. þÿ Alan, made in the form of his Divine Creator, who was created to grace and adorn nature, is not there either amid the wild forest trees or the ruinate but once cultivated fields. Jamaica, with an extent of country that could furnish employment and food for three millions op souls, has not a population of 500,000 ; nay, we doubt if there are even four hundred thousand. This is the chief source, of all her misfortunes. Having arrived at this point of our argument, it may be as well for us to advert to that, which has called forth our remarks on the question of Immigration. A gentleman who is connected with a firm in this town has, we are credibly informed, entered into arrangements with another party, a Madeiran

merchant, we believe, to send one thousand immigrants from Maderia to Jamaica, part of whom, 400, are to be sent on by the 1st of Feb. next, nnd remainder by the 1st of May followirg, þÿ provided (lie immigrants can be þÿhad. Now, we say, all honor be to him who confers a benefit upon his country, and whether the man be friend or foe, we should, indeed, prove ourselves unworthy Scions of the fourth Estate, if we did not þÿ render unto Caesar, the things that are Caesar's." If we applaud the State when the Government propound some measure, which is for the benefit of a Country; how much more necessary is it, that we should render homage to the exertions and energy of an individual subject of that State, who devotes his time and stakes his hard earned capital upon the development of a Government plan. But there are other causes which render the act still more commendable. Madeira lias been sadly afflicted with Divine visitations of recent years þÿ the blight by which the crops of grapes have been destroyed, has produced an unusual amount of want and destitution; and were it not for the foreign aid that has been afforded, from time to time, the people in that Island must have perished by thousands, from the want of food. But the greatest blessing that can possibly be bestowed upon a starving people, is, to afford them the means of earning a subsistence þÿ and that is the aid which our fellowtownsman þÿI hincas Abraham, Esquire, has entered into arrangements with some Madeira

gentlemen, to effect. But if there be one cause more than another, which makes us pay homage to Mr. Abiaham, it is this. That a son of the House of Israel shall have entered into arrangements, for transporting one thousand of his Christian brethren who are suffering from want, to another Christian country, there to be provided with the means of earning their subsistence, by the instrumentality of their Hebrew brother. þÿ Trelawny, AW. l?

WILL OF PETER THE GREAT. In the name of the Most Holy and Indivisible Trinity, we Peter the Great, under all descendants and successors to the throne and government of the Russian nation. The Ail-Powerful, from whom we hold our life and our throne, after having revealed to us his wishes and intentions, and after being our support, permits us to look upon i Russia as called upon most graciously to establish her rule over all Europe. This idea, is based upon the fact that all the nations of this portion of the globe are fast approaching a state of utter J decrepitude. From this it results that they can be easily conquered by a new race of people, when it has attained full power and strength. We look on our invasion of the West and East as a decree of Divine Providence, which has already once regenerated the Roman empire by an invasion of barbarians. The emigration of men from the North is like the inundation of the Nile, which at certain seasons enriches with its waters the arid plains of Egypt We found Russia a small rivulet, we have it an immense river. Our successors will make of it an ocean, destined to fertilise the whole of Europe, if they know how to guide its waves. We leave them, then, the following instructions, which wc earnestly recommend to their constant meditation : þÿ 1. To keep the Russian nation in constant warfare, in order always to have good soldiers. Peace must only be permitted to recruit the finances. To recruit the army choose the moment favourable for attack. Thus peace will advance

your prospects of war, and war those of peace, for obtaining the enlargement and prosperity of Russia. 2. Draw unto you, by all possible means, from the civilized nations of Europe, captains during war, and learned men during peace, so that Russia may benefit by the advantages of other nations. 3. Take care to mix in the affairs of all Europe, and, in particular, of Germany which, being the nearest nation to you, deserves your chief attention. 4. Divide Poland by raising up continual disorders and jealousies within its bosom. Gain over its rulers with gold ; influence and corrupt the Diet, in order to have a voice in the election of the Kings. Blake partisans, and protect them ; if neighbouring powers raise objections and opposition, surmount the obstacles by stirring up discord within their countries. 5. Take all you can from Sweden ; and, to effect this isolate her from Denmark, and vice versa. Be careful to rouse their jealousy. 6. Marry Russian Princes with German Princesses ; multiply the alliances ; unite these interests ; and by the increase of our influence attach Germany to our cause. 7. Seek the alliances with England, on account of our commerce, as being the country most useful for the development of our navy (merchants, tje. ) and for the exchange of our produce against her goods ; keep up continued communications with her merchants and sailors so that ours may acquire experience in commerce and navigation 8. Constantly extend yourselves along the shores of the Baltic and the borders of the

Euxinc. 9. Do all in your power to approach closely Constantinople and India. Remember that he who rules over these countries is the real Sovereign of the world. Keep up continued wars with j Turkey and with Persia. Establish dockyards in the Black Sea. Gradually obtain the command of this sea, as well as of the Baltic. This is necessary for the entire success of our project. Hasten the fall of Persia. Open for yourselves a ! route towards the Persian Gulf. Re-establish as much as possible, by means of Syria, the ancient commerce of the Levant, and thus advance towards India. Once there, you will not require English gold. 10. Cnrofully seek alliance of Austria. Make her believe that you will second her in her projects

3 T IB a X A'HS for dominion over Germany, and secretly stir up the jealousy of other Princes against her, and manage so that each be disposed to claim the assistance of Russia ; and exercise over each a sort of protection which will lead the way to future domination over them. 1 1 . Make Austria drive the Turks out of Europe, neutralize her jealousy by offering to her a portion of your conquests, which you will further on take back. 12. Above all, recall around you the schismatic Greeks who are spread over Hungary and Poland : become their centre and support þÿ as universal dominion over them, by a kind of sacerdotal rule (autocrat sacerdotal) ; by this you will have many friends amongst your enemies. 13. Sweden dismembered, Persia conquered, þÿPo and subjugated, Turkey beaten, our armies united, the Black and Baltic Sea guarded by our vessels, prepare separately and secretly, first the Court of Versailles, theu that of Vienna, to share the empire of the universe with Russia. If one accept, flatter her ambition, and amour proprt , and make use of one to crush the other, by engaging them in war. The result cannot be doubtful if Russia will be possessed of the whole of the East, and of a great portion of Europe. 14. If, which is not probable, both should refuse the offer of Russia, raise a quarrel between them, and one which will ruin them both. Then Russia, profiting by this decisive moment, will inundate Germany with the troops which she will have assembled beforehand. At the same time,

two fleets full of soldiers will have the Baltic and Black Seaþÿ will advance along the Mediterranean and the Ocean, keeping France in check with one and Germany with the other. And these two countries conquered, the remainder of Europe will j fall under our yoke. Thus will Europe be sub- ! jugated.

The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Friday the 10M February 1854. We ventured to offer a few remarks, i a short time since, on the high prices, in this Island, of all provisions; with the only view of modifying it possible, the avaricious propensity manifested by merchants, shopkeepers, and lastly, though not least, by bakers; but, without any effect. High prices are yet retained, and in fact, increased on many necessaries of life; because the demand becomes greater day by day. Our intercourse with St. Thomas, whence supplies were received, is now unhappily interrupted, and may continue, God knows, for a longer time yet. The community is consequently entirely dependent on merchants and shopkeepers, whose stock may be large enough to meet the demand until our intercourse with St. Thomas can be renewed ; or a supply be received

elsewhere; but doubtless at such a very exorbitant rate as to preclude the possibility of the necessaries of life being obtained by the poorer classes. This, we consider, would be an evil of very great magnitude; and hope that such a calamity may not befall this community. It is, however, proper to guard against such an evil; and we, in behalf of the poor, would therefore call on the proper authorities to exert that aid they are wont to practise on all occasions that demand their attention and assistance. A supply of provisions obtained from America, on the public account, and retailed here in lots at such a price as would cover cost and expenses þÿ is the only remedy we can offer.

From the London Morning Herald, January 7, 1853. The writers and journalists þÿ even though domiciliated in Downing-street þÿ a locality sacred of late to solemnity, stupidity, and Scotch metaphysics þÿ the writers who oracularly proclaim that Oscar, King of Sweden, has Russian sympathies and leanings, must judge the Scandinavian Sovereign as a þÿ man made after their own þÿhearts, and not as he really and truly exists þÿ that is to say, a perfectly independent entity. So far as personal sympathies and predilections go, the Sovereign of Sweden is the most of a Frenchman and the least of a Russian of any crowned head in Europe. We might go further and say, that he is personally hound up with the Bonaparte family, being a kinsman and connection of the eldest of the race þÿ Joseph Bonaparte. The mother of King Oscar of Sweden was Mdlle. Desiree Clary, daughter of a rich merchant of Marseilles, and the sister of this lady, who so long presided over the Court of Stockholm, had previously married the eldest of the Bonaparte family. Independently of this brotherhood between the families of Bonaparte and Bernadottc, Oscar of Sweden does not forget that by the direr tion of the Emperor Napoleon he received his early education at the I.yeee Imperial, where he had for tutor one of the staunchest partisans of the Emperor, M. Champagne, under whose care the boy remained ti'l he had obtained bis eleventh year. Many there are in Paris at this moment who well remember the young Oscar Bernadottc in 1S09 and 1810, and who little considered at

that early epoch that the youth with the Ossianic name was so soon destined to assume the title of Duke'of Sudermania, and ultimately to ascend the throne of Sweden. Though, before he was twelve years of age, young Oscar Bernadottc was a pupil i of the Swedish scholar, poet, and journalist, Atterbom, one of the editors of the Srensk Literatur Tedning and the Skandia, yet in becoming the scholar of this celebrated professor of the University of Upsala, the young Bernadottc learned to love the spirit and patriotism of his adopted country, without forgetting the land of his birth. The lessons of patriotism and independence instilled into his mind by his first professor were fortified, and, to use the language of Lord Bacon, þÿ þÿcorroborated by the Count of Cederstrom and by the learned and celebrated Taunstrom, one of the most patriotic men in a land fertile with the honest and brave. As Chancellor of the Swedish University, which he in timo became, the present King of Sweden was certainly not likely to be Russianised, for if there be a class in Sweden which loathes tie Mus covite systom more than another, it is the senate, professors, and alumni of the Swedish universities. In subsequently occupying high ranks in both arms of the Swedish service, neither tho soldier nor sailors under þÿOscar command s ever concealed

the hereditary antipathy both entertain to the oppressors and spoliators of Norway and Finland, and the tyrants and partitioners of Poland, formerly an appanage and ally of Sweden. Nor could the marriage of Oscar Bernadotte act otherwise than to deepen the intensity of his antipathy to Russia. His father-in-law, Eugene Beauharnois, Duke of Leuchtenberg, had practical experience of the Punic faith of Russia, and the eldest daughter of Eugene, the present Queen of Sweden, was brought up cherish her þÿfather s years ago to opinions and convictions. Josephine, the Queen of Sweden þÿ for she was baptised in the name of her grandmother the Empress Josephine þÿ is a great favourite with the Swedish people, and her four sons have rendered themselves popular by warmly professing those opinions dear to Scania and to the honest yeomen and peasants of Darlccarlia. It may be answered that on the second occasion in which the present King of Sweden left his country, he travelled to Russia, and visited the Court at St. Petersburgh. It is undoubtedly true, that while Grand Admiral of Sweden and Norway Oscar visited St. Petersburgh in 1830; but a complimentary visit of this kind was a mere formal ceremonious piece of civility. As such it was intended by Charles John XIV., and as such it was received by the Emperor Nicholas. In 1834, as Viceroy of Norway ; in 1835, 1836, and 1837, as a member of various administrative committees; in 1838, as regent of the kingdom ; and from 1 844 to 1 854 as King of

Sweden, Oscar has shown that he is neither to be cajoled nor to be intimidated by the threats or the wiles of Russia. For near ten years the march of the Swedish Government has been at once independent, liberal, and national, favourable to the extension of a patriotic spirit, and, as a consequence, antagonistic to the system of Russia. The people, though not rich, are frugal and industrious; and their Monarch, with few wants, and the son of a soldier of fortune, nevertheless inherited from his father, late King, a fortune of 80 millions of francs. Five years before his accession to the crown the reigning Sovereign became a princely, if not a royal author. In 1839 he published a remarkable dissertation on the education proper to be given to the Swedish people ; and in 1841 an essay on penal laws and reformatory establishments. Is it likely that a monarch of this stamp and character, whose army, whose navy, whose landed proprietors, whose merchants and whose bankers detest the name and policy cf Russia, would at this crisis betray the interests confided to him, and also recede from the opinions of his past political life. The wish that he may do so possibly rises in the bosom of þÿ The classic thane þÿ Athenian þÿAberdeen. But such an idea never once entered the mind of Oscar, nor would it bo congenial to any of the heroes of Ossian, who were neither feeble nor faithless in their generation, however some of the Piets descended from him may have degenerated. Though we cannot speak as favourably of the

King of Denmark as the King of Sweden, yet of this we arc quite sure, that the people of Denmark have just as laudable a horror of the principles, policy, and state system of Russia as the people of Norway and Sweden. So much for national and personal feeling in a question now of European concernment. That Russian intriguers have lately been busily at work both at Stockholm and Copenhagen we are well aware. But we do not believe that the declaration of neutrality lately issued by these two Courts has been colourably or corruptly made in the interest of Russia, or that it can subserve those interests if fairly and honestly persevered in. It is notorious to all the jurists of the world that the principles and the practice of England and of Russia have ever been at variance as to the question of the flag covering the cargo, and the Swedes

3 tL\ ATJ8. and the Danes know this fact too well to make goods. Russia, always fraudulent and always dishonest, does, no doubt, vehemently desire to protect her commerce by thus carrying it on in neutral bottoms, or, in other words, under the protection of the Swedish and Danish flag. But such a system cannot be allowed by England or France, for the whole policy of our maritime code is against it. The same jurisprudence that prevailed fifty at þÿDoctors Commons, under the greatest of modern civilians, Sir William Scott, rules and prevails also in the American Courts of Admiralty ; and the case of the Liesbet, the Susa, the Yigalantia, and Heaven knows how many others, argued and decided in the Prize Courts and Cockpit here, are sound law at New York and Washington. It is, however, we repeat, an injustice to suppose that either Sweden or Denmark will not continue, as they profess to be, strictly neutral. The duties of a neutral are comprised in the observance of the strictest impartiality between the contending parties, and in not affording succour or assistance to either belligerent. England and France need no succour or assistance ; and if either of the neutrals afford it to Russia they will be condignly punished, not merely by the scorn and contempt of their own subjects, but by the swift and summary justice of the two most civi- | lised and the two most powerful nations of the j world.

The Peninsular and Oriental þÿCompany screw s steamer, Himalaya, arrived at Southampton on Friday forenoon from London. She left London on Thursday morning, and averaged during her voyage about 14 miles an hour. The Himalaya is the largest ship in the world, and is intended for the conveyance of the mails between Southampton and Alexandria A large party, consisting of many of the directors and other chief persons connected with the Peninsular and Oriental

Company, with their friends, came round to Souththeir ships colourable conveyers of an þÿenemy s ampton in the Himalaya. It was thick weather on Friday over Southampton Water, but about midday a huge mountainous mass emerged from the fog near the dockbuoy, which was immediately made out on shore to be the Himalaya. She hoisted a signal for the docks, and steaming up the Itcben river, entered the dock with perfect ease, and soon came alongside, occupying and filling a berth which is usually occupied by two large steamers. A large crowd of persons assembled in the docks to witness her arrival. While in the centre of the dock her huge but beautiful proportions could be seen to advantage. Although Southampton people are accustomed to see monster steamers, the amazing length and bulk of the Himalaya struck every one with surprise. She is ship rigged, not heavily so, and she drew 15 feet of water forward, and 18 feet aft. Of course she is light now, but, when she is heavily laden, and deeper in the þÿwater the fineness of her lines will be more conspicuous than at present. On stepping on board, her vastness was again evident. She has a flush deck, and if a person, walking up one side of it and down the other, travels over her length seven times, he walks a mile. She is nearly as long as Bernard-street, a wellknown street in Southampton, which has on one side of it 22 three-storeyed houses with spacious shops. Her width is as great as many a large metropolitan street. Her depth is enormous.

The funnel is 24 feet in circumference, and is scarcely noticed on the deck. A person at one end of the deck hallooing ever so loud could not be heard distinctly at the other end. Relays of officers will communicate the orders of the commander to either end of the ship. On the platform where the commander is stationed, there are a series of bells to communicate with the engine department. On the Himalaya entering Southampton Water, Calshot Castle, the ancient defence of that entrance, and the Solent looked like a molehill when contrasted with the steamer, and could have been stowed away þÿ guns, artillery, men, and all þÿ in her hold. Nearly 200 passenþÿgers berths are onboard of her, 150 of which are first class, with rooms as large as those at hotels ; 200 persons can dine luxuriously in the saloon. The fittings-up of the steamer are superb and the þÿ upholstery work is most expensive. All the curtains cost three guineas a yard, and damask five guineas. The þÿladies saloon is a large, elegant, and commodious apartment, with þÿservants room and bath room adjoining. The Himalaya is an iron shifi, built by Mare, and cost about £150,000. She would have cost much more had she been built of wood. The engines are by Penn, and are the direct acting trunk engines, such as were fitted into some of the screw line-of-battle ships, the Agamemnon for instance. They work beautifully, and will give immense speed. The Himalaya will bring Gibraltar within three days distance, Malta six days, and Egypt nine days. She would

take 2,000 soldiers a distance as far as the Cape of Good Hope in about three weeks, and 2,000 emigrants to America in a week. This magnificent vessel is as yet the crowning effort of a princely enterprise. The appearance and success of such a colossal steamer has been foretold, but never before realised. There can be no doubt now that the great ocean will be bridged over by steamers like the Himalaya before long ; at present, however, that vessel is one of the wonders of the world. þÿ Obseever, Jan. 15.

From Wilmer and Smith's European Times, January 16, 1854. The Chinese Labourers in the West Indies.

A Government return has just been issued describing the results, so far as they have yet been ascertained, of the recent experiment for introducing Chinese immigrants to compete with Coolies and Africans as labourers in Guiana and Trinidad, in both colonies the plan appears to have been attended with as much success as could have been anticipated. No proper care was originally taken in the selection of the men ; they were landed without any interpreters to make their wants known, or to enable them to receive instruction in the duties required of them in a stiange country, and their entire number consisted of males ; yet, in almost every case where it was not rendered impossible by the ill effects of the voyage, they went to work at once with cheerfulness, and subsequently displayed a tractability such as to show that, under fair circumstances, they would prove the best labourers the colonies ever possessed. The first arrivals in Guiana took place in January last, and consisted of about 350 persons, followed by an additional 300 in March. After three þÿmonths experience numerous reports were received regarding them, and the general testimony, notwithstanding many doubts previously entertained, was unanimous as to their being equal to the Coolies, while, in a majority of instances, they were greatly preferred. One proprietor writes þÿ þÿ 1 am better pleased with them than any class of immigrant, and my experience for the last five years has been þÿvaried. Others state

that they would þÿ rather have one Chinese than two Coolies, as they consider their physical strength þÿgreater. Their eagerness to earn money causes them to be disappointed even at not being allowed to work on Sundays, yet with this vigour of the acquisitive propensity they unite a taste for luxury in food and clothing which leads to a free consumption of imported articles. From Trindad the accounts are of a similar character. The first arrival in that island consisted of 432 in March last, followed by 251 in April, and 305 in July. In the course of a few weeks the planters reported that they were highly pleased with them, and described them as more intelligent than the African, and cleanlier, healthier, and stronger than the Coolie. þÿ 1 must þÿsay, observes an old planter, þÿ that during upwards of 30 þÿyears experience 1 never saw people more willing to do their work than these þÿmen. Here, also, their tendency to lay out their money in poultry, pigs, and clothing was soon manifested, and it was regarded with the more satisfaction, inasmuch as it would not only promote the general welfare of the colony, but would afford a counter-attraction to rum drinking, þÿ for which they show a rather stronger predilection than might have been predicated from þÿtea-drinkers. From these facts it will be seen that, considering the disadvantage they must have sustained from their inability to understand the language of their employers, and also that a large number of them, including several conformed opium eaters,
were such as should never have been sent, while even the healthy were in many instances, from the old neglect of ventilation on board ship, landed in the last stage of feeble-

f AT I 8 ness after the death of a large percentage of their companions, there is every reason to assume that further experience will cause their introduction to be regarded with increased satisfaction. That their capacities and conduct may be open to some objections is to be inferred from the circumstance of one of the local newspapers of Guiana being especially hostile to them, although its reiterated averments that they were proving an expensive failure seem to have been contradicted in every case by the employers themselves. It is admitted to be true that they are prone to violent combinations, but only when their peculiar feelings are not respected. At other times they are docile and amenable to authority, and, although some had been committed to gaol for theft, desertion, and refusal to labour, the cases of that description were few and exceptional Among their recommendations is their adroitness in the use of new implements, which the African would resist. The pains they take to finish their work well, and the fact that their houses are þÿ models of cleanliness and order," likewise go far to account for the statement that all those who have employed any of them are ready to take more. At Guiana it is hoped for the future to introduce 1500 a-year, half the expense being paid by the colony and half by the planters. In Trinidad a resolution has been adopted for an additional supply of 300 in the current year, of whom one-half are to be women. Whether the present rates of freight, however, will admit

of these importations on the terms contemplated is doubtful. The commissioners in London advertised, a few months back, for ships to convey 1800 Chinese emigrants to Jamaica and Guiana, but were unable to obtain them at a rate that could be afforded. At the same time the number of Chinese who are desirous of getting the opportunity of emigrating on the condition offered appears to be without limit. Whether women could equally be obtained is contested by some, on the ground that the practice of female infanticide in China reduces the proportion of the sexes, while their habit of crippling their feel renders them unfit for labour and locomotion, Other persons, apparently on better authority, affirm that there would be no difficulty on the subject. Upon this question in some measure depends the continuance of the movement, since, unless those who arrive out can be induced to settle permanently, the probability is that its cost would be found too heavy.

TURKEY. Turkey requires no more aid in the assertion of its independence from the Allied Powers than the United Provinces did from Elizabeth, yet assuredly the independence of Holland was for centuries no þÿ contradiction in terms " Turkey needs less aid in the assertion of its independence now than Belgium did in 1830. The aid which Turkey craves at the hands of the Western Powers is not of that nature or extent that could palliate their wresting the sceptre from the hands of the Sultan, and reigning in his stead. Nor, if it did, could such a policy promote the civilisation and hapiness of Turkey. No country can be civilised or rendered prosperous by an alien government; only by their own efforts can a people be made free and happy. þÿ Observer, January 15.

Napoleon anti flic lSn««iaiiM. The Battle of Friedland. It was on the 5th of June 1807, that the storm of war commenced. Bay and night it continued unabated, as the Russians, fighting with desperation, sullenly retreated before their fees. On the 10th, the allies had concentered, upon the field of Hcilsberg, on the banks of the River Alle, 90,000 men. Here they planted themselves firmly behind entrenchments, fortified by five hundred pieces of heavy artillery. These were loaded tj the muzzle with grape-shot, to mow down the French, advancing over the open plain. In utter recklessness of life, 30,000 Frenchmen, rending the skies with their wild hurrahs, rushed upon the muzzles of these guns. Murat and Ney headed the desperate assault. Napoleon was not there to witness a scene of butch cry so inexeusablo. The Russian batteries opened upon the bare bosoms of these moving masses, and whole heads of columns wore swept away. Still on and on the impetuous host rushed, with oaths and shouts, wading through blood, and trampling over piles of the slain. They pour over the entrenchments, sabre the gunners, shout victory. Suddenly, the tramp of iron hoofs is heard. Trumpets sound the charge. A squadron of horse, ten thousand strong, sweeps down upon the French with resistless plunge. The shout of victory sinks away into the wail of death. The French who had scaled the ramparts were overwhelmed, annihilated. Thus the tide of battlo ebbed and flowed all day long. Night came. Dense volumes of smoko canopied the field of

demoniac war with the sulphurous gloom of the world of woe. By the light of the þÿcannon s flash the surges of battle still rolled to and fro. Clouds gathered in the black sky. A dismal rain began to fall, as if nature herself wept over the crimes of the children of earth. Midnight came. The booming of the guns gradually ceased, as the soldiers, utterly exhausted with a conflict of twelve hours, threw themselves amidst the dying and the dead, upon the stormdren hed and gory ground. Late in the night Napoleon came galloping upon the field. He was exceedingly displeased at the senseless butchery to which his impetuous generals had led the men. The dawn of a gloomy morning of wind and rain revealed to both armies an awful spectaclo. Tho two hostile hosts were within half cannon shot of each other. The narrow space between was covered with eighteen thousand of the dead and wounded. All the dead, and many of the wounded, had been stripped entirely naked by those wretches, both male and female, who ever, in great numbers, follow in the wake of armies for such plunder. These naked bodies, crimsoned with gore, mutilated by balls and by ghastly sabre strokes, presented an aspect of war stripped of all its pageantry. By mutual, instinctive consent, both parties laid aside their guns, and hastened to the relief of the wounded and to the burial of the dead. How strange the scone! Russians and Frenchmen were now mingled together upon the same field, in perfect amity, vying with each other in deeds of

kindness. Each army then resumed its position to renew the fight. The Russians rallied behind their en'renchments ; the French upon the open plain. Napoleon, ever anxious to spare the needless effusion of blood, so skilfully manoeuvred, preparing to attack his foes in the rear, that tlio Russians were soon compelled, without the firing of a gun, to abandon their position, and to continue their retreat. All the night of the 12th of June the Russians were precipitately retiring Though dreadfully fatigued, they continued their flight the whole of the next day. They were compelled to make another stand upon the plain of Friedland. Their doom was sealed. Napoleon had driven them into the elbow of a river, and had so skilfully drawn together his forces, as to render their escape impossible. Early in the morning of the 14th, the battle of Friedland commenced. The division of Lnnnes was in the advance. The Russian army fell upon it with the utmost energy, hoping to secure its destruction before the other divisions of the French army could come to its relief. Napoleon was ten miles distant when bo heard the first deep boomin'; of the cannon. Ho sent in every direction for Ii is battalion to hasten to the scene of conflict. At noon Napoleon galloped upon the heights which overlooked the field. As he saw the position of the enemy, hemmed in by the bend of the river, and bis own troops marching up on every side, a gleam of joy lighted up bis features. þÿ This, he exclaimed, þÿ the is 14th ef Juno. It

is the anniversary of Marengo. It is a lucky day for þÿus. The French, during the morning, had been contending against fearful odds. Lannes, with 26,000 men bad withstood the assault of the whole Russian army of 80,000. As Napoleon appeared upon the heights, General Oudinot, plunging bis spurs into bis horse hastened to the Emperor, exclaiming, þÿ Make haste. Sire ! My grenadiers arc utterly exhausted. But give me a reinforcement, and I will drive all the Russians into the þÿriver. The clothes of the intrepid soldier were perforated with balls and his horse was covered with blood. Napoleon glanced proudly at him, and then, with his glass, carefully and silently surveyed the field of battle. One of his officers ventured to suggest that it would be best to defer the battle for a few

hours until the rest of the troops had arrived and had obtained a little rest. þÿ No, no þÿ! Napoleon replied, energetically. þÿ One does not catch an enemy twice in such a þÿscrape. Calling his lieutenants around him, he explained to them his plan of attack, with that laconic force and precision of language, which no man has ever surpassed. Grasping the arm of Marshal Ney, aud pointing to the little town of Friedland, and the dense masses of the Russians crowded before it, be said emphatically. þÿ Yonder is the goal. March to it without looking about you. Break into that thick mass, whatever it costs. Enter Friedland ; take the bridges and give yourself no concern about what may happen on your right, your left, or your rear. The army and l shall be there to attend to þÿthat. Ney, proud of the desperate enterprise assigned him, set out on the gallop to head his troops. Napoleon followed with his eye this þÿ bravest of the þÿbrave. Impressed by bis martial attitude, be exclaimed, þÿ That man is a þÿlion. þÿNey division s of 14,000 men, with a solid tramp which seemed to shake the plain, hurled itself upon the foe. At the same signal the whole French line advanced. It was a spectacle of awful sublimity. One incessant roar of battle, louder than the heaviest thunders, shook the plain. Napoleon stood in the center of the divisions which ho held in reserve. A large cannon ball came whistling over their heads, just above the bayonets of the troops. A young soldier instinctively dodged. Napoleon looked

at him, and smiling, said, þÿ My friend, if that ball were destined for you, though you were to burrow a hundred feet under ground, it would bo sure to find you þÿtheie. Friedland was soon in flames, and Ney in possession of its blazing dwellings, aud its bloodstained streets As the darkness of night came on the scene was indescribably awful. The Russians, having lost 25,000 men in killed and wounded, retreated toward the river, pursued by the victorious French, who were plowing their ranks incessantly with grape-shot, musketry, and cannon balls. The bridges were all destroy'd!. A frightful spectacle of wreck and ruin was now presented. The retreating army plunged into the stream. Some found fords, and wading breast high, reached the opposite bank, and planted anew their batteries; thousands were swept away by the current. The shore, for miles, was lined with the bodies of drowned men. A storm of bullets swept the river, crowded with the fugitives, and the water ran red with Hood. The allied army was now utterly destroyed. It was impossible to make any further opposition to the advance of Napoleon. The broken bands of the vanquished retired precipitately across the Niemen, and took refuge in the wilds of Russia The Russian generals and the Russian army now clamored loudly for peace. Alexander sent a messenger to Napoleon, imploring an armistice. Napoleon promptly replied, that after so much fatigue, toil, and suffering, he desired nothing so much as a safe and honorable peace :
and that most cordially lie consented to an armistice, hoping that it might secure that desirable end Thus in ten days the campaign was terminated. þÿ Harper's Magazine.

EXTRACT from a lecture of Horace Marin, delivered be fore the ' Boston American þÿLibra y Association" entitled þÿ A Few Thoughts for a Young Man " ' I Becin with the postulate, that it is a law of our nature to desire happiness. This law

is not local, hut universal ; not temtorary, but eternal. It is not a law to be proved by exception, for it knows no exception. The savage and the martyr welcome fteice pains, not because they love pain, but because they love some expected remuneration of liappi t ess so well, that they are willing to purchase it at the pi ice of the pain ; at the price of nnpii s' nmert. tor'ute, ot death The young destte happiness mote keenly than any otheis This desite is innate, spontaneous, exuberant j and nothing but repealed and repeated overflows ol the la' a of disappointment can burn or bury it in their liiensts. On this law of our na- 1 in e. then, we may stand as on an immovable foundation of truth Whatever foitune may befall our aigurncnt, our premises are secure. The conscious desire of happiness is active in all men. Its objects are easily conceivable by all men. But, alas! towards what ililTerent points of the moral compass do men lock lor these objects, and expect to find them. Some lock lor happiness above, and some below ; some in the grandeur of tire soul, and some hi the grossness ol the sense ; some in lire heaven of puriiv, and some in i he hell of licenciotisness. Wherever H is lor kerf for, the imagination adoies it with all its glowing colours. Multitudes of those who seek for happiness will not obtain the object of their search, beause they seek it amiss. Deceived bv false ideas of its nature, oilier multitudes, who obtain the object of their search, will find it to be sorrow and not joy, þÿ Dead Sea ap-

ples, and not celestial fiuits. Whether a young man shall reap pleasure or pain from winning the objects of his choice, depends not only upon his wisdom or folly in selecting those oljeets; hut upon the right or wrong method by which fie pursues them. Hence, a knowledge what to select and how to pursue, is as necessary to the highest happiness as virtue herself. Virtue is an angel, but she is a blind one, and must ask of knowledge to shew her the pathway that leads to her goal. Mere knowledge on the other hand, like a Swiss rnercenery is ready to combat either in the ranks of sin or under ihe banners of righteousness; ready to forge cannon balls or to print New Testaments ; to navigate a þÿoonrsei svessel or a missionary ship. But however energetic and vast the desires of happiness may be, þÿ swelling in millions of hearts, glowing on enjoyment, | and growing still more on disappointment. þÿ nothing is more certain than that t he range and possibility of happiness, which (Jed has provided, and placed within nrm's length of us all, is still vaster than the desire of it, in any ami in all of his creatures We are finite, and can receive only in finite quantities ; He is infinite, and gives in infinite quanties. Look outwardly, and behold the variety and redundancy of means which the Creator has prepared to meet and to satisfy all the rational wants of his children. So ample and multitudinous are the gifts of God ! that he needed immensity of space for their storehouse ; and so various are they, and ascend-

ing one above another in their adaptation to our capacities of enjoyment, that we need an eternity to set out the banquet. If the human heart can ever find any rational excuse for repining. it is not liccause of the penury and cheerlcssncss of its lot ; but because as it mounts above in its reach after higher enjoyments. it is compelled to leave such pure and exquisite pleasures untasted behind it. From the Observer, February 12, 1854. MILITARY. On Thursday night orders were received at the Infantry barracks, Windsor, for 350 rank and file of the second battalion of Scots Fusilier Guards to hold themselves in readiness to embark on Thursday or Friday next. It is understood that similar drafts will be made from other battalions of Foot Guards, making a magnificent brigade of 2,500 strong from the Grenadier, Coldstream, and Scots Fusilier Guards. The Guards will march from Windsor under the command of Lieut. -Col. Dixon, direct to the port of embarkation. On Friday morning a party of 21 of the Fusiliers, accompanied by several non-commissioned officers, were despatched to different parts of the country on the recruiting service, and in order to facilitate the enlistment of men, the standard height of recruits has been lowered one inch and a half. The object is to increase the force of the regiment (two battalions) to 1,600 strong. The first division of the 62nd Regiment embarked at Queenstown on Thursday, on board the Sir Charles Pollock, transport, for Malta ; and, on the day preceding, the first division of the 9th Regiment was put on board the Canterbury transport, and sailed for the Mediterranean. The 90th Regiment is shortly expected at Cork for embarkation ; and the 50th, which passed through Cork, en route from Plymouth to Dublin, has been ordered back, in order to take shipping for the Mediterranean. The 46th Regiment, stationed at Kilkenny, under orders for Australia, is countermanded, and remains on home service ; and a

large draft of the 40th will leave to join the service companies at that colony. On Friday notices from the Admiralty were posted on þÿ Change, at Lloyds', and in the various coffee-houses, one of which was to the effect that on Friday next, the 17th inst., they will be ready to receive tenders for the hire of steamers for the immediate conveyance of troops to Malta, the owners victualling the troops ; and another intimating that on Tuesday next, the 14th, the Admiralty will also be ready to treat for the hire of seven or eight good coppered ships of from 5C0 to 700 tons, new measurement, to be employed as regular cavalry transports for four months certain, and, if required, fora longer period. The Government has chartered the Peninsular and Oriental þÿCompany s steamers Himalaya, Ripon, and Manilla for the conveyance of troops. The three vessels will carry about 3,500 soldiers. The troops will be victualled by the company. The steamers Sultan and Euxinc will be employed in conveying the Indian, China, and Australian mails to and from Southampton and Alexandria during the time the Ripon and Himalaya arc employed in the transport of troops. The number of troops to be dispatched at once is 10,000 officers and men. But as many more will be held in readiness to reinforce the British contingent, should necessity demand their services in the East, it is possible the following will proceed on the 18th or 19th: þÿ 3 battalions of the Guards, 7th Regiment of Foot, 28th Regiment of Foot

33rd Regiment of Foot, 79th Regiment of Foot, 2nd Battalion of Rifles, 4 companies of Artillery. The others will follow as soon as the transports can be got ready. It is also intended to send out three regiments of cavalry At least twenty steam-ships of the largest tonnage will be required to convey troops and supplies. The Government have, therefore, claimed the services of the contract mail steamers, the exigencies of war being paramount to all other considerations. The only troop-ships in England arc the Simoom, Vulcan, Bulldog, and Dragon. Each of these, however, could carry 1,200, and the þÿwho c of them together nearly 5,000 troops. WOLFF St. Thomas, 6th March, 1854. þÿ þÿ000« FRANC lb Louis Napoleon has addressed the following admirable Letter to the Emperor of Russia, and it is hoped that his good intention will be received by the Czar : þÿ þÿ Palace of the Tuileries, Jan. 29, 1854. þÿ þÿ Sire, The difference which has arisen between your majesty and the Ottoman Porto has arrived at such a point of gravity, that I consider it a duty to myself to explain directly to your Majesty the part which France has taken in this question, and tho means which I conceive to bo calculated to avert tho dangers which monaeo the repose Europe. of

þÿ The note which your Majesty has just had presented to my government and to that of Queen Victoria endeavours to establish that þÿ the system of pressure adopted, from the outset, by the two maritime Powers, has alone envenomed the quesþÿtion. But the matter would, on the contrary, it appears to me, have still continued a Cabinet question, had not the occupation of the Principalities transported it all at once from the domain of discussion into that of facts. However, once that the troops of your Majesty had entered Wallachia, we not the less recommended the Porte not to consider that occupation as a casus belli, thereby giving proof of our extreme desire for conciliatory measures. After having concerted with England, Austria, and Prussia, I proposed to your Majesty a note calculated to give a common satisfaction ; your Majesty accepted it ; but scarcely were we informed of that good intelligence when your minister, by explanatory commentaries, destroyed all its conciliatory effect, and prevented us thereby from insisting at Constantinople on its adoption without any alteration. On its side, the Porte had proposed in the note certain modifications which the Four Powers, represented at Vienna, considered of a nature to he accepted ; but the changes in question did not meet with the approbation of your Majesty. Then, the Porte, wounded in its dignity, menaced in its independence, and straitened by the efforts already made to raise an army in opposition to that of

your Majesty, preferred declaring war to remaining in that state of uncertainty and abasement. The Porte had applied for our support; its eauso appeared to us just ; and the English and French squadrons received orders to anchor in the Bosphorus. þÿ Our attitude with respect to Turkey wa3 protecting but passive. We did not encourage it to make war ; but, on tho contrary, incessantly gave to the Sultan counsels of peace and moderation, persuaded that that was the only means of arriving at an arrangement, and the Four Powers again came to an understanding to submit to your Majesty other propositions. Your Majesty, on your side, displaying the calm which originates in tho consciousness of force, had confined yourself to repelling, on the left Bank of the Danube as in Asia, the attacks of the Turks ; and, with a moderation worthy of the head of a great empire, had declared that you would remain on the defensive. Up to that point we were, therefore, I must declare, interested spectators, hut still nothing but spectators of the contest ; when all at þÿTidcnde. once the affair of Sinope occurred, and forced us to assume a more decided attitude. Franco and England had not considered it advisable to send troops to be landed for the assistance of Turkey, and their flag consequently was not engaged in the conflicts which had taken place on land. But by sea the case was different. There were at tho mouth of the Bosphorus three thousand pieces of cannon, tho presence of which declared plainly

enough to Turkey that tho two first naval powers would not allow any attack to be made on her by sea. Tho affair of Sinope was for us as offensive as it was unexpected ; for it is a matter of little importance whether tho Turks intended or not to land stores and ammunition on the Russian territory. In fact, the Russian ships-of-tho-lino came and attacked Turkish vessels of smaller force in tho waters of Turkey, and while tranquilly anchored in a Turkish port, and they destroyed them, notwithstanding the assurance given not to wage an aggressivo war, and notwithstanding tho vicinity of our squadrons. It was no longer our policy which there reoeived a check ; it was our military honor. The cannon shots of Sinope produced a doop fooling of affliction in tho hearts of all who in England and in France have a lively sontiment of the national dignity. With a common accord tho cry aroso everywhere that, þÿ whorever our cannon can reach, our allies must bo þÿrespected. Tbouco emanated tho ordor given

3 t o our squadrons to enter the Black Sea, and to prevent by force, if necessary, the recurrence of such an event ; and thence, too, the collective notification sent to the Cabinet of St. Petersburg, to the effect that if we prevented the Turks from carrying on aggressive war on the coasts belonging to Russia, we would protect the sending of stores and ammunition to their troops on their own territory. As to the Russian fleet, in interdicting it from navigating the Black Sea, we placed it in different conditions, because it was important during the continuance of the war to preserve a pledge which might be an equivalent for the parts of the Turkish territory which were occupied, and might facilitate the conclusion of peace by becoming an object in an exchange which was so much to be desired. þÿ Such, Sire, is the manner in which events have followed each other and been connected together ; and it is clear that having arrived at this point, they must promptly lead either to a definitive understanding, or to a decisive rupture. þÿ Your Majesty has given so many proofs of your solicitude for the repose of Europe, and contributed so powerfully by your beneficent influence to put down the spirit of disorder, that I cannot entertain any doubt of the resolution which you will come to in the alternative presented to your choice. If your Majesty desires as ardently as I do a pacific conclusion, what is more simple than at once to declare that an armistice shall be signed forthwith, that matters shall resume their

diplomatic course, that all hostility shall cease, and that all the belligerent forces shall be withdrawn from the places where motives of war have called them ? þÿ In that case, the Russian troops would quit the Principalities and our squadrons the Black Sea. As your Majesty prefers to treat directly with Turkey, you would name an ambassador to negotiate with a plenipotentiary of the Sultan, respecting a convention which should be submitted to the Conference of the Four Powers. Let your Majesty adopt that plan, on which the Queen of England and myself are perfectly in accord, and tranquillity will be re-established and the world satisfied. There is, in fact, nothing in this plan that is not worthy of your Majesty, nothing that can wound your honor. But if, from a motive difficult to be comprehended, your Majesty should refuse, in that case, France, as well as England would be obliged to leave to the fate of arms and to the hazards of war what might be decided at present by reason and justice. þÿ Let not your Majesty suppose that the slightest animosity can enter my heart ; it experiences no other sentiments than those expressed by your Majesty in the letter which you wrote to me on January 17, 1853. þÿ Our þÿrelations, you said, þÿ ought to be sincerely amicable, and ought to be based on the same intentions þÿ namely, maintenance of order, respect for treaties, love of peace, and reciprocal kind þÿfeeling. That programme is worthy of the Sovereign who traced it out, and I

do not hesitate to declare that I have remained faithful to it. þÿ I request your Majesty to believe in the sincerity of my sentiments ; and it is in such sentiments that I am, Sire, your þÿMajesty good s friend, þÿ NAPOLEON. þÿ Ibid, March. 1 1 .

Remedies against Pride. Cast your eyes on yourself, and yon will there find motives enough of humility. Do but consider what you were before you were born, what you are since you have been born, and what you are like to be after your death. Before your birth, you were a filthy matter unworthy to be named ; at presont you aro a dunghill covorcd with snow, and in a short time will be meat for worms. What have you now, Oman, to be proud of? You whose birth is sin, whose lifo is misery, and whoso end is rottenness and corruption ! If the temporal

© :» ® s a: A'n s. riches you possess are the subject of your pride, stay but a moment, death will come and make us all equal. For as we are all born equal as to our natural condition, so we shall all die equal according to the common necessity of maukind, with this only difference, that they who have had the most here, will have the largest accounts to make up after death. Consider seriously the graves of the dead, and find, if you can, the least marks of all that splendor and magnificence they lived in, or of the riches and pleasures they enjoyed Tell me now what is become of their rich furniture and costly clothes ? where are all their sports and pastimes ? what have they done with all their servants and attendants ? their sumptuous entertainments, their merriments, their jests and worldly mirth are now all over : Do but go near any one of their graves, and you will find nothing but dust and ashes, with worms and rotten bones. This, therefore, is the end their bodies are to come to, how þÿtender and y nicely soever they have been treated. And I wish there were no evil beyond or greater than this. But this is not all : there is something follows, that is much more to be apprehended; it is the dreadful tiibuual of the Divine Justice, the sentence which will be passed there, the weeping and gnashing of teeth, the never-dying worm, which bites and gnaws the consciences, and the fire which shall never be extinguished. Consider the danger of vain-glory, þÿpride daugh- s ter. For this reason you ought, whenever men

commend or respect you, to consider immediately whether you really have those qualities they commend you for or not. For if you have not, you have uo reason at all to be proud ; but it you should perhaps have them, say with the apostle, þÿ the By grace of God I am what I þÿam. So that you have no reason to be proud on that account, but, on the contrary, to bumble yourself, and to praise God, to whom you are indebted for all you have, that by this means make yourself | not unworthy of what he has been pleased to bestow on you ; for it is certain, that the respect which men pay to you, and the reason for their doing so, comes from God ; and, therefore, you rob God of as much honor as you appropriate to yourself. Can any servant be more unfaithful than he that steals his þÿmaster glory s ? Consider, further, what a folly and madness it is to rate your worth and merit according to the opinion and esteem of men, who have the liberty of turning the scale which way they please, of taking away in a short time what they now give you, and of stripping you of the honor they at present afford you. II you j build your reputation on what they say of you to- 1 at day, perhaps you will be a great man, as mean to-morrow, and next day nothing at all ; just as a company of inconstant and changeable men shall think fit to talk of you. Your business, therefore, is, never to value yourself on the commendations others give you, but only on what you know of yourself. And though they should cry you up to

the very skies, hearken at the same time to what your conscience says, and be persuaded, that you are better acquainted with yourself than other men arc, who have only a distant view of you, and can judge of you by nothing else but by what they hear. Take no notice of what men say or think of you, but commit your honor and glory into þÿGod shands ; he is wiso enough to lay it up for you, and faithful enough to give it you back again. Consider also, 0 ambitious man, what dangers the desire you have of commanding others exposes you to. For this reason the Scripture says, þÿ That those who are tho ministers of justice shall have severe sentence passed against them, and that tbo mighty shall be mightily þÿtormented. Besides, who is ablo to express tho cares and troubles thoso persons live in who have many others to look after ? We havo an excellent example hereof in a certain king, who, just as ho 1 was going to bo crowned, took tho crown in his hands before they placed it on his head, and, hav-

ing looked steadfastly on it for a while, cried out, þÿ 0 crown, much more thorny than rich ! if a man did but know tliee thoroughly, he would never stoop to take thee up, though he found thee lying on the þÿground. Consider once again, 0 proud man, that your pride is acceptable to no person. It is not acceptable to God, because ho is your enemy; for þÿ he resists the proud, and gives grace to the þÿhumble. It cannot but be odious to the humble, because every body sees what a horror they have of any thing that is proud and haughty ; nor will those who are themselves as proud as you like it, because they hate you on the very same account that you value yourself, and can endure none that is greater than they are. And what is worst of all, you will never be satisfied with yourself in this world, if you do not but enter into yourself and reflect on your own vanity and folly ; and you will have much less contentment in the next world, when you shall be condemned, in punishment of your pride, to eternal torments. God coufiruis this by the mouth of St. Bernard, when he says, þÿ 0 man, if you were but thoroughly acquainted with yoursell, you would bo disagreeable to yourself, and thereon agreeable to me ; but for want of knowing yourself, you are puffed up with pride, and therefore it is that I hate þÿyou. The time will cotne when you will neither please yourself nor me ; you will not please me, because of the climes you have committed, nor yourself, because of the torments you shall be condemned

to for all eternity. There is none but the devil, that approves your pride ; it was this changed him into a most hideous and deformed spirit, from a most glorious and beautiful angel ; and, therefore, it is natural to him to be pleased when he sees others like himself.

The following useful article, illustrating the danger of practical jokes, by the following anecdote, is related by a party to the sad incident : þÿ A WtGKR. In the town in which my friend was born and brought up, and which has since merged into a portion of the vast metropolis Britain, of a few young gentleman who had distinguished themselves at school, and were now engaged in acquiring various professions, formed themselves into a literary association, which met twice a-wcek at the house of a friend. Basesnd, 20th March 1854. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Dear Sir, At the fourth meeting of the Colonial Council in 1852, a bill was introduced, having for its object the extension to theso Colonies of the laws regarding Religion which arc in force in Denmark. This bill þÿ on account of the inward connexion and affinity of the two þÿmatters, so says the Report of the Proceedings of that Council, was referred to the committee appointed on the subject of the extension of the law of 13th April 1851, regarding Marriages. Tho report of this Committeo was in due time delivered: when Lo! Tho committeo had forgotten to say one word on this matter of inward þÿ connexion and affinity þÿ! What is most remarkable, is this, that the mover of this bill was himself a member of the committeo ! ! ! The Colonists therefore, at the present moment, aro yet bound to obey those stringent laws of tho mother country which aro exactly one hundred years behind the ago. In tho mother country where, it is notorious, that indifferentism in religious matters prevails to a great extent, an enlightened Policy has annulled these laws and granted liberty of conscience ; while in these Colonics, whore, expressed as in the Report of tho Committee þÿ greator veneration for church institutions is to be found than in the mother þÿcountry and where from this reason liberty of conscience, ono should think, is more desired the straightened policy of Colonial Legislation

presents the Anomaly of a Constitutional Government without liberty of conscience. But it might not he out of place to give bore an outline of these laws, annulled in Denmark, but in full farce in these Colonies. In the Danish Law 2nd Book 1 Chap., we read þÿ þÿ That Religion only shall be permitted in the Kingdom which agrees with the Holy Bible, the Apostolic, Nieene and Athanasian Creeds as also with tho Augsburg Confession and þÿLuther little s Catheþÿchism. This law has, in course of time, devel- so oped itself, that there could scarcely be a doubt that all persons of foreign religions could obtain permission, not only to reside in the kingdom, but also to worship God privately in his own peculiar manner. On the other hand it is entirely prohibited, that those who belong to the National Church should leave that church and attach themselves to any other ; and it is also decreed, that every child of parents belonging to that church is by birth its Bondman. The Reformed Churches are prohibited from making Proselytes of those who belong to the Lutheran Religion. They are charged (Privil. 15th May 1747 4) that they shall not make any endeavours, directly or indirectly, to draw any to their Religions, and that they, when any ono of his own freewill , offers himself to bo admitted to their Religions, shall not receive such a one , but shall turn him away. þÿ In the 14 it is also ordained that those children, the issue of mixed marriages, between the Lutheran and Reform-

ed Churches shall be brought up in the Lutheran Religion. This latter injunction was afterward so altered, that it should be decided on by tho Parties to which church their children should be brought up þÿ and in case no such decision has been made, then the boys shall bo brought up in the þÿFather Religion s and the girls in the þÿMother s. From the above alone, it is evident that although the National Church, as a rule, permits Persons of other Persuasions to reside in the kingdom, yet they must on no account, induce the members of that church to come over to theirs ; or, as the Law would express it to fall into þÿ þÿHeresy. The National Church in these Colonies is therefore an enclosed something, to which there are many Entrances, but from which there is no other lawful outlet than through the Portals of Death. It will be out of place here to say anything regarding the institution of a National Church ; þÿ þÿbut as a writer on Political Philosophy observes þÿ the confining of the subject to the. religion of the state is a needless violation of natural liberty, and is an instance in which constraint is always grievous. Persecution produces no sincere con. viction, nor any real change of opinion : on tho contrary, it vitiates the public morals, by driving men to prevarication, and commonly ends in a general though secret infidelity , bv imposing, under the name of revealed religion, systems of doctrine which men cannot believe, and dare not examine ; finally, it disgraces tho character and

wounds tho reputation of Christianity itself, by making it the author of oppression, cvuelty and þÿbloodshed. I cannot avoid quoting a few observations, which I translate from a danish pamphlet, written on tho Baptist Question, which question was agitated in Denmark, before tho promulgation of the Constitution. The writer observes : þÿ It is not out of place in our days to remark, that the church of the state is a Community resting on its own conviction, and that it is through or by this conviction that its members are bound to it. It is this spirit, for which alone the church should caro ; he who iD his soul has forsaken the church, is no longer in the church ; and when wo nevertheless demand that he shall continue in it, we act in the same manner as if tho state should demand of her þÿ dead subjects that they shall continue to bo its þÿsubjects.

The writer again observes : þÿ It is therefore very remarkable, that the state has been go mine as to declare, that the State-Church would suffer considerable loss, and perhaps even dissolution if the Bondmen of the church were granted the right to leave it. If this fear were well grounded, it would be a perfectly sufficient and plain declaration that all our ecclesiastical relations are hollow ; that the internal life of the church is extinct and that the church þÿ has sunk from a living Organism, to a dead Machine, the component parts of which are only kept together by punishments the of the þÿlaw. Again : þÿ When a member of the church is obliged to reason thus: I am born in the State-Church, and I am thereby bound to it for my whole life ; even if my convictions should lead me to another religious community þÿ if I even should thereby satisfy my þÿsoul demands, s it would still be useless to think of any change, because the knot which my birth has tied, my convictions cannot loosen. þÿ When a member must thus think, (and so must all the members of the State-Church think) then such a thought exercises a dull somniferous power over the soul, which crushes many an endeavour to obtain a more clear and living conviction, and there remains behind in the soul, an undefined darkness, and an unsatisfied feeling, which often goes over to þÿIndifferentism. This accounts for the religious indifference so much deplored in Denmark, and which even manifests itself in the State-Church here.

Intolerant laws similar to these, and even more stringent have existed in England, but during tho progress of enlightenment, they were repealed ; and that as early as in 1689; from which period religious toleration in England may be dated. Thus at the very time when England was striking off the shackles, which fettered the consciences of men, the mother country was fettering them on. But these laws have been annulled in Denmark. Why should they then remain in force here ? Have tee no consciences ? Do we not worship tho same God þÿ should we not be as free to do so as our brethren in the mother country ? Let us then trust that the subject may again be brought before the Colonial Council, if not by Government, by a member : but let us also hope that that member will do something more than merely introducing such a bill. þÿ A comprehensive national þÿreligion says Palcy þÿ guarded by a few articles of peace and conformity, together with a legal provision for tho clergy of that religion ; and with a complete toleration of all dissenters from the established church , without any other limitation of exception than what arises from tho conjunction of dangerous political dispositions with certain religious tenets ; appears to be not only the most just and liberal , but ike wisest and safest system which a state can adopt ; in as much as it unites the several perfections which a religious constitution ought to aim at þÿ private judgement , with the care of the public j of truth , with the peace of society ; the right of conscience , with means of instruction ; the progress safety þÿ. I remain, dear Sir
þÿYour truly s A. From the Morning Herald, Feb. 28. 1854. TURKEY AND RUSSIA.

Drouyu do j Lhuys, to the representatives of France at Foreign , two English lieutenants of Engineers, and a Courts, informing them of the alliance which has 1 been contracted between England and France, in view of the common danger. This alliance will have the effect of protecting all interests that war may endanger, and therefore French agents are directed everywhere to protect and assist English vessels and English subjects, in the same manner, and as if they possessed the same rights, as French vessels and French þÿsubjects. Eslo perpetua. Tho union of England and France is the guarantee for universal national independence, and for the peace of the world : þÿ Tho Monitcur also publishes a decree prohibiting exportation the of arms of every description, and also of gun-stocks, projectiles, and other munitions of war. Clothing, horses, sailing-vessels, and steamers also conic under the prohibition. þÿ The Monilenr further publishes a letter from Prince Napoleon to the Emperor, in which the Prince requests permission to form part of the expedition which is being prepared þÿ The same official journal announces the armament of a third squadron of 10 ships of the lino, 14 frigates, and 15 corvettes, composed of sailing

and steam vessels, under the command of Admiral Parse val þÿDcschencs. Orders have been received at Toulon for tho embarkation of tho troops destined for the East. þÿ A dispatch from Vienna, received at Paris on Saturday evening, fully confirms the ndhesion of liberty of | the Government of Austria to the policy of England and þÿFrance. The following is tho latest intelligence from the Austrian capital : þÿ VIENNA, Feb. 23. þÿ The events connected with the war now leave no hope of a pacific arrangement. The Emperor has ordered an additional force of 25,000 men, which has already taken up a position in tho Banat, and also 25,000 men to protect the south-eastern frontier, or to be employed as circumstances may require. þÿ Tho French Ambassador has received dispatches from Athens which announco the extension of tho Greek insurrection in Turkey. BUCHAREST, Feb. IS. þÿ The cannonade of tho Russian batteries against Rustchuk þÿcontinues. ODESSA, Feb. 13. þÿ The troops of the government of Twer, Ostrowa, and Jaroskffhavc marched for the Danube,

and will pass through Moscow. There are neither English nor French vessels at Odessa. þÿ Letters from St. Petersburgh, of the 16th, inform us that the Russian courier, bringing intelligence to that government of Baron Brunow and M. de Kisseloff having actually demanded their passports, arrived 24 hours before the French and English couriers, bearers, of the instructions to tho representatives of those Powers to demand theirs. The consequence was, that the Emperor acted on the intelligence brought by his couriers, and, without permitting the time to pass which would have allowed of the arrival of the French and English couriers, scut their passports to Sir Hamilton Seymour and General de þÿCastelbajac. Nicholas has, ly a public decree, cashiered tho Emperor of Austria and King of Prussia, who had condescended to accept tho command of regiments in his service as colonels þÿ Russian officials, military and civil, are forbidden to wear any insignia which they may havo received from the Sovereigns of either Austria or þÿPrussia. A silly outbreak of ill-temper. þÿ Letters from Moscow state that tho war is not popular there. French colonel, with an adjutant, arrived at the Turkish capital on the 9th, on board the Caradoc. On the 11th they visited the Dardanelles, to inspect the þÿfortifications. The Greek insurrection is said to bo extending, but the reports upon the subject arc vague and obscure.

It is not impossible that Russia may soon he indulged with an insurrection of its own in tho very heart of the Empire. Tho new conscription has excited great discontent at Moscow and in its neighbourhood, and not without reason. Tho Emperor and the Imperial Treasury hare lately suffered much pecuniary embarrassment. Upon this subject a contemporary observes : þÿ þÿ Of course, these pecuniary embarrassments are greatly increased by the de facto stoppage of the British trade ; for, as no remittances havo been made from this country to Russia this winter for tho purchase of raw produco in that country, the ordinary courso of trado i3 as effectually stopped ns if the blockade of the Russian ports had already commenced. The landowners who arc the growers of this produce find their market cut off ; the agents who conduct the business aro without their usual remittances ; and all the innumerable transactions of private life which depend on this periodical arrival of foreign capital are suspended. The Russian government, however, not taking into account tho enormous inconvenience and dissatisfaction caused to the class of landed proprietors by this state of affairs, has proceeded to inflict on them two measures of a still more serious character. By a ukase of tho 10th of February, the Emperor has ordered a levy of no less than 9 men on every 1000 souls throughout the western governments of tho empire, to commence on tho 1st of March and to finish on tho 15th of April, and by a special provision tho
Jews subject to the conscription are to furnish 10 per 1000, instead of þÿ9.

Tho levy will withdraw about 300,000 serfs from productivo labour ; and in addition to this, another arbitrary decree reduces by one-third tho number of days to bo devoted to forced labour ; hut as really all labour in Russia is compulsory, this is a reduction of at least 30 per cent, of tho productivo labour of the empire- This looks liko madness.
