We Inve since received the Asmonean, which, besides several notices of his life, culled from other papers, contains also his will. We select some of the notices, and reprint the will in cxlenso, it being u most remarkable document, deserving to be recorded in a Jewish journal: þÿ The venerable Judah Touro departed this life on Wednesday night, at his residence in Canal-street. New Orleans has thus lost one of her best citizens þÿ charity one of its sincerest devotees, and humanity one of its truest friends. Mr, Touro had attained the advanced age of 79. Fifty of these years were passed in New Orleans, and every one of that fifty was marked by some good act. Embarking in mercantile enterprises about the time of the cession of Louisiana, Mr. Touro continued peiseveringly and industriously in the pursuit of independence, until, by regular nnd legitimate accumulation, he became wealthy, and died leaving an estate of over a million. But, though earnest and successful in the prosecution of business, Mr. Touro was never a selfish or close man. On the contrary, ho has for many years been the furemost of our rich men in all contributions to charitable objects. Some of iris donations have been on a scale of magnificence nnd liberality which are scarcely paralleled in cur country. We j may instance a few of these. Henring, some j years ago, that the Bunker Hill Monument

was retarded in its completion by the want of twenty thousand dollars, and that a liberal citizen of New England had offered to unite with any other citizen in giving ten thousand dollars for this object, he sent his check for the amount ; and the monument was completed. For many years, Mr. Touro was the owner of the very valuable property next to the St. Charles Hotel, which was occupied by Mr. Clapp as the First Congregational Church. Though the property was susceptible of being made immensely productive, being in the centre of the business portion of the city, he permitted Mr. Clapp to continue in possession of the church, and in the enjoyment of the rents of the pews, until it was destroyed by fire. He then purchased another very valuable lot, in a moro eligible location for a church, and donated it to the Mr. Clapp. The merits of this liberality will be more highly appreciated when it is known that Mr. Touro was of the Hebrew persuasion, and a strict obsorver of that ancient faith and worship. He was, indeed, one of the great props of that faith in this city. Besides this, ho has contiibuted largely to all the churches in this city, of every denomination, and has for many years sustained a synagogue, which was erected at his expense, in his native town of Newport, 11. I , for the uso of his brother Israelites. It would be an interesting record, if it

donations to charitable nnd religious institutions. But such record will never be discovered, for ho was, of all men who ever possessed the means, most distinguished for that charity which Does good by stealth, blushing te find It fame.

He preferred to administer h>s charity in his own the bank, just as it was left by his brother. fashion, and after the dictates of his own heart nnd judgment. Thus his nets not unfrequently had an aspect of eccentricity. We that came into our port, and was passionately remember once being called on by some Christian missionaries from Jerusalem, for the purpose of directing attention to an appeal which they were making to the American people for assistance in supporting the persecuted Christians in that remote quarter. When asked to whom they might present their appeal, with the best chance of a liberal response, we answered, " Judah T þÿouro. But he is a Jew ; nnd it would be going far to ask a Jew to aid in the establishment of Christianity in the capital of the þÿJews, was ' the reply. Nevertheless, we persisted in our recommendation. The result confirmed our judgment of the good old man. He gave ten limes more than any Christian in the city to aid the cause of Christianity in the land of Judea. Air. þÿTouro s career as a citizen nnd a patriot was consistent with his character as a

his country, a sincere republican. Though no politician, he had great faith in the doctrine of þÿman e s quality and capacity for his own government. He knew no distinction between men. and was ever the sincere friend of the labourer, the artisan, and the poor man. His hand was ever extended to aid and encourage youthful energy and enterj prise. As a patriot he had suffered severely in the defence of the soil and honour of his country. On the 1st of January, 1815, whilst serving in one of the militia regiments of the city, under Jackson, he was selected, on account of his trustworthiness, to aid in carrying the cartridges from the magazine in the rear of the lines to Col. Humphrey's battery. Whilst thus engaged, with the balls of the British flying thick around him, Air. Touro was struck in the thigh with a twelve-pound shot, which produced a ghastly wound, tearing off a large mass of flesh. He was taken up from the ground by his old friend and constant associate for the last fifty years. U. L). Shepherd, and brought to the city, in what was believed to be a dying condition. But after incredible suffering, being confined to his bed for twelve months, Air. Touro recovered, nnd though ever after slightly lame, enjoyed remarkable health. This was due to habits of extraordinary regularity and systematic incongregation of dustry. He never drank a drop of spirits or j vinous liquors in his life; never omitted to ; rise with the dawn of day, and to retire at an I early hour.

In his religious observances, Air. Touro was exceedingly exact nnd punctual. There were eccentric traits in his character, which, though of a perfectly innocent nature, were quite remarkable. From rhe hour of his arrival here, he had never passed beyond the limits of the city but once, and then it was to fight under Jackson in the defence of the city. He could never be persuaded to travel in any vehicle sinco the could be obtained, that of all Air. þÿTouro s death of a beloved brother, who was thrown out of a carriage in Boston, and had his leg broken. That brother bequeathed him 100,000 dols., which were deposited in one of the banks of Boston. The money was permitted to remain in the bank without interest t and Mr. Touro could never be per-
suaded to receive or use a dollar of it. Tho sum stands now to his credit on the books of
Though he had a New þÿEnglander fondness s for ships, and owned some of the largest craft

fond of talking nbout ships, ..oir Lost mode of structure, and took a great pride in tho beauty and neatness of his own cruft, he could never be persuaded It) go aboard of one of them, but would content himself by standing on the levee, and viewing in s:lent admiration the hoge hulks, the tapering masts, and snowy sails of his great cotton ships. But our sketch has already extended beyond our limits. It is not often a community loses so valuable a citizen, society so good a man, as Judah Touro. Of all the amiable traits of his character, none were more commendable and beautiful than his modesty nnd simplicity. He moved through the struggling crowds of humanity with the noiseless tread of one who seemed not wrapt in the eager pursuit of gain, of ambition, or selfish pleasure, but as one who lived only to benfit humanity, to accumulate a fund from which philanthropist. He was ardently devoted to might flow copious and fructifying streams of charily and beneficence. He was the owner of splendid edifices nnd magnificent stores, but only retained one small apartment and a corner in an office for himself þÿVV ithout any blood relations or other domestic ties, lie made all humanity his family, and lavished his care and liberality upon all who were in need, nnd who wero deserving. Air. Touro was the last of the four richest of our citizens who have died in this city during the last four years without families. John AlcDonough, Joseph Fowler, and Cornelius Paulding w ere the other three. The

combined fortunes of these four citizens reached the sum of nine millions, a! out one-cigf.th of the property of the whole city. They were all bachelors, and lived to an extreme old age. Air. McDonough died nt 72, Air. Paulding at 70, Mr. Fowler nt 05, ai d Air. Touro at 79. They all had been constant residents at New Oi leans, nnd enjoyed a rcmatkable degree of health and vigour. Except Mr. Fowler, the shortest-lived of the four, none of them had ever left the city. And now, by far the best of them has just been gathered unto Aloges and the Prophets. May the virtue and goodness of his life bo requited by tho bliss of that better world to which his soul has ascended, and may his memory be ever cherished as that of one of the truest of philanthropists and pat riots ( We could multiply these extracts were it necessary to show the estimation in which tho deceased was held by those who knew him well, but we must rest here, adding but one little notice, selected from many communications which have been sent us on the þÿsubject. SWEDEN. Stockholm, Feb. 14. þÿ The secret committee was last Saturday empowered by the King to mako a statement to the full Diet respecting the exterior affairs. The neutrality of Denmark and Sweden had been approved by tho German Powers, and acknowledged by France and England ; but Russia, whilo assenting to the neutrality of Denmark, had raised difficulties respecting Sweden. Diplomatic ncgociations were still pending for the duo maintenance of tho resolve taken by the King, but they were of such a nature as to precludo all publicity for the present. Lastly, tho King intended to demand a grant for tho adoption of measures of a naturo to maintain tho neutrality declared conjointly with Denmark. Tho prevailing sentiment is universal indignation against Russia. In tho ports of Norway there are being equipped two frigates, three corvettes,
snr atis, and a division of the coasting fleet. The increase to be made to the Swedish army is not yet fixed.

EXTRACT from a lecture of Horace Mann, delivered before the þÿ Boston American Library Associaþÿtion, entitled þÿ A Few Thoughts for a Young Man" (Continued from No. 1065.) Man not a savage or a pauper by the in- is exorable fatality of his nature, lie is surrounded with every form of the truest and noblest wealth : þÿ wealth, or well-being, for the body, wealth for the mind, wealth for the heart. He is not of plebeian origin, but his lineage is from God ; and when he asserts and exemplifies the dignity of his nature, royal and patrician titles shrink into nothingness, and sink to oblivion Men were not created to perform twenty four months bodily labour in twelve months of time, while the intellectual and moral improvement, which a single year might muster, is spread over a life The laws of nature and of God doom no man to live on a potatoe n day ; but the productive powers of the earth are as much beyond all the demands of healthful sustenance, as the volume to the atmosphere which encircles the globe is beyond the capacity of human lungs. Men were not created to live in wigwams n >r in sties; but to rise up and lie down in dwellings of comfort and elegance. Men were not created for mendacity, societies, and alms houses, and the gallows, but for competitions, and freedom, and virtue ; not for thoughtless puerilities and vanities, but for dignity and honour, for j ty inexpressible and full of glory. See how the means of sustenance and comfort are distributed and diversified throughout

the earth. There is not a mood of body, from the wantonness of health to the languor of the death- bed, for which the wonderful alchemy of nature does not proffer some luxury to stimulate our pleasures, or her pharmacy some catholicon to assuage our pains. What textures for clothing þÿ from the gossamer thread which the silkworm weaves to silk like furs which the winds of Zembla cannot penetrate I As materials from which to construct our dwellings, what Quin cies and New llampshires of granite, what Alleghanies of oak, what forests of pine, belt ing the continent ! What coalfields to supply (he lost warmth of the receding sun I Naked ness and famine and pestilence arc not inex orible ordinances of nature. Nudity and rags arc only human idleness or ignorance out on exhibition. The cholera is but the wrath of God against unclcanlmess and imempe inncc. Famine is only a proof of individual miscon duct, or of national misgovernment. In the woes of Ireland, God is proclaiming the wickedness of England in tones as clear and articulate as those in which he spoke from Sinai, and it needs no hebraist to translate the thunder. And if famine needs not to be, then other forms of destitution and misery need not to be. llut amid the exuberance of this country, our dangers spring from abundance rather than from scarcity. Young men, espe cially young men in our cities; walk in the midst of allurements for the appetite. Hence health is imperiled ; and so indispensable an element is health in all form of human wel-
fare, that whoever invigorates his health has already obtained one of tho great guarantees of mental superiority of usefulness, and of virtue Health, strength, and longevity, de-

pend upon immutable laws There is no charge about them. There is no arbitrary interference of higher powers woh them. þÿ1 iimaiily our parents, and secondarily ourselves. are responsible for them. The providence of God is no more responsible, because the virulence of disease rises above tho power of all therapeutics, or because one quarter part of the human race die before completing the age of one year, þÿ die before completing one seventieth part ol the term of existence allotted to them by the þÿpsalmist; 1 say the providence of God is no more responsible for these things, than it is for picking pockets or stealing horses. Were a young man to write down a list of his duties, health should be among the first items in the catalogue. This is no exaggeration ot its value, for health is indispensably necessary to almost every form of human enjoyment, it is the grand auxiliary to usefulness ; and should a man love the Lord his God with all his heart and soul and mind and strength, he would have ten times more heart and soul and mind and strength to love Him with, in the vigour of health, than under the palsy of disease. Not only the amount, the quality of the labour which a man can perform, depends upon his health. The work savours of the workman. If the poet sickens, his verse sickens; if black venus blood flows, to an þÿauthor brain, s it beclouds his pages ; and the devotions of a consumptive man scent of his disease, as lord þÿByron obscenities s smell ot gin. Not only þÿ lying þÿlips, but a dispeptic stomach, is an abo-

mination to the Lord. At least in this life so dependant is mind upon material þÿorganization, tho functions and manifestations of tho soul upon the body it inhabits, þÿ that the materialist hardly states practical results too strongly, when lie affirms that thought and passion, wit, imagination and love, are only emanations from exquisitely organized mailer, just as periume is the affluence of flowers, or music the ethereal product ol an eolian harp. In regard to the indulgence of appetite, and the man. agement of the victual organs, society is still in a state of barbarism, and the young mail who is true to his highest interests, must create a civilization for himself. The brutish part of our nature governs the spiritual. Appetite is Nicholas the first, and the noble faculties of mind and heart are Hungarian captives. Were we to see a rich banker exchange eagles for coppers by tale, or a rich merchant birtersilk for sergo by the pound, we should deem them worthy of any epithet in the vocabulary of folly. Yet the same man buy pains whose prime cost is greater than the amplest fund of natural enjoyments. Their purveyor and market-men bring them home headaches, and indigestion, and neurology by hamper full3. Their butler bottles up stone, and gout, and tho liver complaint, falsely labelling them sherry, or madeira, or port, and the stultified masters have not wit enough to see through the cheat. The mass of society look with envy upon the epicure who, day by day, for four hours

luxurious eating suffers twenty hours of sharp aching ; who pays a full price for a hot supper, and is so pleased with the bargain that he throws in a sleepless and tempestuous night, as a gratuity. English factory children have received the commisseration of the world, because they were scourged to work eighteen hours out of twenty-four; but there is many a theoretic republican who is a harsher þÿI haroah to his stomach than this; þÿ who allows it no more resting time than he docs his watch ; who gives it no Sunday, no holy-day, no vacation in any sense. Our pious ancestors enacted a law that suicides should be buried where four roads met, and that a cart load of stones shouTd be thrown upon the body Yet when gentlemen or ladies commit suicides, not by cord or steel but by turtle soup and lobster salad, they may be buried in consecrated ground, and under tho auspices of the church, and the public are not ashamed to read an epitaph upon their tombstones false enough to make the marble blush. Were the barbarous old laws now in force that punished tho body of the suicide for the offence which his soul had committed, wo should fu.d many a Mound auburne at the cross roads. Is it not humiliating and amazing, that man, invited by the exalted pleasures of the intellect, and the sacred faculties of the heart, to como to a banquet worthy of the gods, should stop by tho wayside to feed on garbage, and to drink of the Syrian cup that transforms them into swine ! Fatal Duel at Constantinople. þÿ A melancholy affair of honour took place on the 4th, at the great burying ground, between two French officers, Marsaux and Mouginot, both professors and comrades in the Military Academy. They fought with swords, and in less than five minutes Mouginot fell mortally wounded, the weapon ot his antagonist having traversed both lungs. He was a young offier ot great promise þÿ his knowledge and attainments various, and of the highest order, and his loss has been universally deplored. An inquest was held by t lie French authorities, and it appears that, all having been fairly conducted and according to established usage in the French army, M Marsaux is not amenable to criminal law. He was to start next day for France to join his regiment.

The þÿ AVIS. Christiansted, Tuesday the 28<A February 1854. Our columns have lately been graced with an advertisement, which deserves to he headed in large letters Shame! Shame! We allude to the advertisement of the President of the Agricultural Society. In no other Gentlemen of the House of Commons, country, we believe, will men he found, who, after deliberately subscribing þÿ names to such an institution sup- their ported by contribution of the members only þÿ will allow themselves to he called upon publicly for the payment of their subscriptions. The Society lias not been established long 5 and although its progress has been marked only with the publication of a few numbers of its Report, termed þÿ The St. Croix Agricultural and annual Ploughing Matches ; yet we would rather defer chanting its requiem to some future period. There is, assuredly, more to be ex-

in an Island like this, where attention should not only he paid to the cultivation of Sugar, but many other useful branches of Agriculture. Other objects ought to engage its attention, and we will take upon ourselves to say that but for this bad pro-

would long ago have been thought of. The Society, for instance, cotdd turn its attention to the breeding of Mules. It could offer prizes for the best Milehing þÿ &c. were only a little more public Cow the best draught Oxen, &c. þÿ spirit infused into it's members. Rut, not unlike most useful Institutions which have ceased in its infancy in this Island, we fear that this Society will also he numbered with the things that were, if its present pecuniary embarrassment continues.

OPENING OF PARLIAMENT. TUESDAY, JANUARY 31. Her Majesty left the Palace at two þÿo clock, ami arrived at the House of Lords at five minutes past two, and the members of the House ofCommons having been summoned, her Majesty delivered the following speech, returning to the Palace at twenty-six minutes past two : þÿ THE þÿQUEEN S PEECH. My Lords and Gentlemen, I am always happy to meet you in Parliament, and on the present occasion it is with peculiar satisfaction that I recur to your assistance and advice. The hopes which I expressed at the close of last session, that a speedy settlement would he effected of the differences existing between Russia and the Ottoman Porte, have not been realised, and 1 regret to say that a state of' warfare has ensued. 1 have continued to act in cordial co-operation with the Emperor of the French, and my endeavours, in conjunction with my allies, to preserve and restore peace between the contending parties, although hitherto unsuccesful, have been unremitting. I will not fail to persevere in these endeavours; but its the continuance of the war may deeply affect the interests of this country and of Europe, 1 think it necessary to make a further augmentation of my naval and military forces, with a view of supporting my representations and of more effectually contributing to the restoration of peace. I have directed that the papers explanatory of the negoeiations which have taken place upon this subject shall he communicated to you without delay.

The estimates for the year will belaid before you, and I trust you will find that, consistently with the exigencies of the public service at this juncture, they have been framed with a due regard to economy. British Protestants Abroad. þÿ A deputation from the Protestant Alliance, headed by tho Earl of Shaftesbury and Mr. Kinnaird, M. The memorialists urged the Government to make a determined stand against the aggressive and hostile demonstrations, and argued that no political complication or difficulty could result from its being made distinctly known, that Britain would not maintain diplomatic relations with any state which persisted in denying to British subjects within its territory the free exercise of their religion, with liberty to possess places of worship for their own use, as well as places of interment, and to have the rites of baptism, marriage, and burial performed among themselves, without secrecy. to what took place.
